activity: Mr. William Brett, a village cobbler, at work in his shop in Wonersh making a pair of gold-embossed shoes for the Pope.

te.text:
ENGLI SH VILLAGE COBBLER MAKES SHOES FOR THE POPE.

An Englishman makes the Pope's shoes.
He is Mr. William Brett, the village cobbler at
Wonersh, near Guildford, Surrey.
One day, Dr.Banfield, of the Roman Catholic seminary
in the village, asked Mr. Brett if he would make
some shoes for the Pope. The shoes had to be of
special design like a monk's, but with two straps.
The seams were inlaid with gold braid and the heel
was covered in gold. A gold cross was inlaid
in the toe-cap.
All the embroidery work was also done in the village.
Mr. Brett's family have been shoemakers at
Wonersh for nearly 200 years.
PHOTO SHOWS - Mr. William Brett at work in his
shop at Wonersh, Surrey.
AND January 13th 1938 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672.

activity: spinning a fleece from a local Rhondda Valley sheep on an old spinning wheel while barefoot at an educational settlement

te.text:
STEPHENS. CARDIFF.  31/3/54.
A WELSH SPINNER.
Mrs. Doreen Greenway, of Ton Pentre xxxx finds that an old spinning wheel and modern high-heeled shoes do not go together. 
She is seen barefooted busily spinning a fleece from a local Rhondda Valley sheep at the Maes-yr-haf Educational Settlement at Trealaw, Rhondda. 
Mrs. Greenway, whose husband is a miner at the Gelli Colliery, spends nearly all her spare time at the settlement now that her two children are xxxx grown up.
Her interest at first was in weaving rugs etc, for her own use, but now she makes a lot more for use in the Holiday Centre where any members of the clubs attached to the Settlement in the Rondda may spend their holidays.
File: Indus - TEXTILES - WOOL- SPINNING WHEELS .

activity: Oil search at Formby, showing drilling superintendent John Gibson with earth sample boxes brought up from a boring.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

D H White   13/7/49

Oil search at Formby

13 / Supt, of the Drilling operations
     is John Gibson seen here with sample
     boxes of earth brought up from every
     5ft of boring

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
[illegible strikeout] coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

te.text:
18.12.63.
NEW COAL DISTRIBUTION CENTRE OPENED AT WEST DRAYTON.
MR. RICHARD WOOD, former Minister of Fuel and Power,
today opened a coal depot at West Drayton. The depot is
the first to instrument a new system of coal
distribution that has been worked out by LORD ROBENS,
Chairman of the Coal Board, DR. BEECHING, Chairman of
British Railways, and the Coal Merchants Federation.
Instead of the coal being brought from the collieries to
railway sidings for collection by merchants, it will
in future be carried in block trains and concentrated
in these large depots which will serve areas in London
and other large cities. The West Drayton depot takes
the place of 22 small depots within an eight mile radius.
PHOTO SHOWS.
A view of the hoppers where the coal
merchants fill and load the coal.
KT REID JW/764306

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
19 DEC 1963
PLEASE RETURN
TO

KENT'S OLDEST BLACKSMITH IS 90, BUT STILL WORKS AT
HIS FORGE.

Descended from a long line of blacksmiths who have
followed the craft for three centuries, 90-year-old
Mr. Oliver Firrell is now the oldest blacksmith in
Kent.
Hoary-bearded and wearing a skull-cap, Mr. Firrell
is a picturesque and virile figure as he works in his
forge at Matfield Green, old-world village in the midst
of the Kent hop-fields between Tunbridge and Maidstone.
Mr. Firrell has never smoked in his life but enjoys
a glass of beer.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mr. Oliver Firrell at the anvil under
a spreading walnut tree.
AND August 25th 1938 PN.r.

IN every big city of Britain last night squads of
hastily mobilised police were guarding power
stations, gasworks and reservoirs.

Manchester, Liverpool, Alnwick and Belfast.

alone—that at Willesden, N.W. Liverpool’s nine miles of
docks were closely patrolled. Thames police watched the
river between Woolwich Arsenal and Barking power station.
Enfield Small Arms factory was under guard.
The outrages, Scotland Yard believes, are the work of
terrorist emissaries of the outlawed Irish Republican Army.

te.text:
The Mitchell-Hedges Trophy, to be
presented to the winning Division in
the National Coal Output Competition,
is a solid silver oval bowl, weighing
nearly one hundredweight, 27 inches
across and two feet high. It was
designed by John Flaxman, R.A.,
designer to George III, and was made
by Craftsman Paul Storr in 1815 - the date
of Waterloo. The citizens of Denbigh,
North Wales, presented the trophy to
Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, Bart. for
his military prowess.

The trophy was presented to
the mining industry by the Explorer,
Mr. F.A. Mitchell-Hedges.

The inscription in Welsh may
be translated as:

"This silver bowl in praise of
his military feats was presented
to the sweet and gentle Welshman, Sir
Watkin, foremost man of our land, in
salutation of him, and that his memory
may be cherished."

"An ever present help to the
Crown in the day of need was the
manly Sir Watkin - perfect knight in
the foremost line of descent, dear to
his country and his King".

activity: Testing of Britain's first balloon-shaped gasometer on Canvey Island

te.text:
BRITAIN'S FIRST BALLOON-SHAPED GASOMETER
BEING TESTED ON CANVEY ISLAND.

Britain's first balloon-shaped
gasometer is being tested on Canvey
Island (Essex).
It is designed to offer less resistance
to high winds, and if satisfactory
more of the same type will be built
in other parts of the country.
The gasometer is 45-feet in diameter
with a capacity of 500,000 cubic feet.
It has walls three-quarters of an inch
thick and will work at a pressure
of 50 pounds to the square inch.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Britain's first
balloon-shaped gasometer on Canvey Island.
CLEM July 3rd 1936 P.T.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
'PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672

Chairman and Managing Directors of large
companies throughout the country will this week
be receiving through the post an unusual com-
munication - a piece of rusty metal.

Attached to this will be a message about
National Anti-Corrosion Week (October 14 to 19)
and an invitation to attend Britain's first
"Corrosion Exhibition", which opens at the
Royal Horticultural Society's Old Hall on Tuesday.

Attractive 19-year-old Myrna Brown of
Enfield was busy today preparing this unusual
reminder of the importance of corrosion - which
costs British industry six hundred million pounds
a year.

From:  John Wheatley, Organiser, Corrosion Convention
and Exhibition.

- Office Tel.No: EUS.5911

activity: five typists from Colt Heating and Ventilation volunteering to work extra unpaid hours to assist the national economy

te.text:
FIVE TYPISTS [illegible] their firm yesterday that they would work an extra two and a half hours a week without pay to help Britain's financial position.
Within an hour all their 235 colleagues had volunteered to work the extra time too.
So from Monday the staff at the head office of Colt Heating and Ventilation in Surbiton, Surrey, will start at 8.30 am. each day instead of nine.
Several of the 500 workers at the firm's main factory in Havant, Hants., want to do the same, but they will have to get the approval of the Amalgamated Engineering Union.
Way to wealth
The work-harder move was made in response to a staff memo put out by Mr. Fred Price, the firm's marketing director.
The memo said that if everyone in Britain put in an extra unpaid half-day a week "our balance of payments problem would disappear overnight and very quickly we should once more become the wealthiest country in the world."
The five typists—Valerie White, aged 21, Joan Southwell, 20, Christine French, 17, Carol Fry, 16, and Brenda Mumford, 15, sent a memo back.
It said: "Let us be the first company to start the ball rolling."
The five girls, who earn around £10 a week and type an average of 100 orders daily, think they will manage an extra five orders a day in the extra half-hour.
Fabulous
Colt Heating and Ventilation, annual turnover £3-million, export 30 per cent. of their production.
Mr. Alan O'Hea, the firm's 41-year-old joint managing director, described the idea as "the most fabulous I could imagine." He added: "All the management will be at their desks with them at 8.30 am.
"At Havant we will have to wait for the A.E.U. If they decided to stand in the way that is the end of the matter as far as the factory is concerned."
At the AEU head office in London I was told last night: "There is no one here to make a comment. Everyone is on holiday until Tuesday."
er volunteers (from left): Brenda, Christine, Valerie, Joan and Carol

Copyright: Syndication International
27 Floral Street, London, WC2

activity: the frozen food industry, specifically the promotion of frozen chips and peas

te.text:
DAILY
HERALD
RECEIVED
17 MAY 1962
ART LIBRARY

by BARBARA JEFFERY
LOOK out for a big sales war to get
you to eat frozen chips. Last year
£72million was spent on frozen
foods in Britain. But this is still less
than 2½d. in the £ of our total food
bill.
The frozen food firms believe that they
can double these figures. And they are
banking on the potato to do the trick.
So far peas are the runaway best-seller
in the frozen food market, accounting for
a third of the takings. Sales are still
increasing but there is a feeling in some
sections of the trade that saturation point
may not be far off.
What the industry need is another
basic food that can be promoted as peas
have been. And they think that frozen
potatoes — especially frozen chips — are
the answer.

activity: Miss Margaret Hornby trying out the first computerised homes-for-sale register at Plantation House

te.text:
3-1-68
HOUSE-HUNTING....BY COMPUTER.....

     The first ever computerised homes-for-
sale register is being made available to the public
from tomorrow -Thursday 4th. January. 1968.. With
32,000 houses and flats, valued at more than
£100,000,000 already programmed on the computer,
it is believed to be the largest and most comprehensive
single register of residential properties for sale
ever assembled at one central source. The service
is the brainchild of Homeseekers Computer Services of
7. Buckingham Gate, and initially covers properties
in the Great London Area; and 11 surrounding counties-
Bedfordshire; Hertfordshire; Berkshire; Buckinghamshire;
Essex; Hampshire; Kent; Middlesex ;Oxfordshire; Sussex
and Surrey. Three hundred and forty Estate Agents are
participating. Details of their properties are fed into
the computer. Househunters give details of their
requirements. These details are fed into the computer
and the applicant receives in the post information
on the ten properties most closely corresponding to
his requirements. The computer is an I.C.T. 1900
series owned by Assets Computer Services Ltd..

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- MISS MARGARET HORNBY, a
director and Secretary of the Company - with the
questions ..and answers.. as she tries out the first
computerised homes-for-sale register, at Plantation
House, Mincing Lane, this afternoon.
          JSS/KEYSTONE      C/13239-2. /4

NEW JOBS FOR THE RHONDDA.

(See Feature Set Intro. No. 251).

New jobs have come to the Rhondda as 23 new factories
have been opened in the valley. During the depression
of the 1930's there was one collier to every 2.7 of the
total population and four men out of ten suffered up to
15 years of unemployment. Now the ratio is one collier
to every 7.6 of the total population and there are
alternative jobs. Not only is the economic future of
the Rhondda on a broader and safer base, but jobs are
available to those who fall victim to the dreaded dust
diseases which can turn a man from the pits at any age
from 20 until he retires.

te.text: Industry - Misc - Workers - Gen - NOT Working Scenes

6 col x 7" DEEP.
( CUT OUT AS
SHOWN. )

nscraig steelworkers celebrate their output record . . cigars supplied by the management
Picture by JACK HAMILTON

1N RUSSIA they would probably have got
the Order of Lenin, or the title "Hero of
Labour." But not in Britain. Notably not
at the Ravenscraig steelworks in Mother-
well, where yesterday the furnacemen
were celebrating their achievement of a
record week's output. There the manage-
ment were quick to reward each of their
workers with the symbol of capitalist
success: a fat cigar.

They could, when you consider it, have
chosen something equally symbolic to
distribute — like yachts, fast cars or
blondes — but there is a limit to what
can be expected from even the most
grateful management.

In one sense, though, the holders of
the Order of the Fat Cigar have some-
thing in common with the Heroes of
Labour. In Motherwell, the management
have rushed in bearing gifts. In Russia,
the state adds a few more names to the
Marxist honours list. And in neither case
does anyone mention money. In Russia,
because it is a deviationist snare. In
Motherwell, perhaps because they have

activity: General view of the vacant Mansionss at the junction of Great Smith Street and Great Peter Street, Westminster, which have been empty for five years.

te.text:
By DENNIS NEWSON
A FOUR-STOREY block of flats which could house
100 people in comfort is standing empty only a
stone's throw from the Houses of Parliament. It has
been empty for more than FIVE YEARS.
Homeless London families have
eyed the block enviously. Scores
of M Ps have made inquiries,
for it is near enough to the
Commons for them to get home
for a meal and back in time for
a division.
And opposite the building on
the corner of Great Smith-street
and Great Peter-street, West-
minster, is another, smaller
block.
For the past 12 months only
one of its 13 flats has been
occupied.
Action was promised last night
by the Westminster City Coun-
cil's assistant town clerk, Mr.
Ronald Chamberlin.
He was meeting bearded 26-
year-old Mr. Henry Pelham, a
director of the Veribest Manu-
facturing Company which leased
the properties just after the war.
A council official said: " We
understand that Mr. Pelham has
consulted architects about reno-
vating the smaller block and
later letting it.
"If this is not done quickly,
the council may well use its
powers of compulsory purchase."
Mr. Pelham's firm was refused
permission to convert the flats
into offices.
It says it will have to spend
£20,000 on the smaller block.
Renovation of the larger block
might not be commercially
worthwhile as the lease has
only 14 years to run.

EMPTY for five
years .. This
is the block of
flats in Westmin-
ster which could
house 100 fam-
ilies. The council
may take action.

TANNER.              D.H.                22.11.61.
EMPTY FLATS. Story:- Newson.
A large block of flats at the junction of Great Smith
Street, & Great Peter Street, Westminster, big
enough to house 60 homeless people has been vacant
for 5 years.
O.P.S. General view of the vacant Mansionss.

DAILY HERALD

activity: Laying out squares of Swiss quartzite in London for use on the Queen Mary's swimming bath.

te.text:
GOLDEN QUARTZITE, STONE THE PHARAOHS USED, 
PREPARED IN LONDON FOR THE QUEEN MARY. 
 
Golden quartzite, a stone that was used 
in the days of the Pharaohs to line 
the tomb of King Tutankhamen, is 
being prepared by a London firm of 
marble craftsmen for use in the pavements 
around the super swimming bath of the 
giant new liner Queen Mary. 
Quartzite is the seventh hardest 
material known. It is non-slip and the 
colour is permanent. For centuries 
quarrying of it stopped but in the 18th 
century, the monks in the Alps began 
to work it again. 
This is the first time in history that 
golden quartzite has been used for a ship. 
Three hundred tons of onyx from North 
Africa and marble from Malta are being 
made into chimneypieces for the Queen 
Mary. 
PHOTO SHOWS:- Laying out squares of 
Swiss quartzite in London for use on 
the Queen Mary's swimming bath. 
      G January 11th 1936 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

Calcraft   Illus. 1983-5236/76286 28.10.43
Rehearsal in the garden of Ridges Farm, Clifton
Hampden for "Who Killed the Squire".Village boys and
girls play in this Propaganda Play.
OPS 9 Five-years-old David Green wears the chef dres
that won him first prize at a village party. His
mother made it from old sheets. In his tray he
carries samples of dressed-up potatoes made by Joyce
Allmond, a 17-year-old girl. Nobody in Clifton
Hampden ever cooks potatoes in any other way but
their skins. All these dishes were cooked thus,
"dressed-up" afterwards. Note Potatoe ducks with
carrot beak, feet; cloves for eyes. Potat o hedgehog
and fried-bread spines. Potatoe baskets contain
Russian salad.  Half potatoes represent boats with
lettuce sails.
After the picture was taken David made sure that
he took tray home. He was going to eat all the
potatoes.

activity: an aerial view of the gigantic oil tanker "British Argosy" at the Swan Hunter shipyard on the River Tyne prior to launching

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S
DAILIES, 24TH JANUARY, 1966

BIGGEST SHIP TO BE BUILT ON THE TYNE WILL
BE LAUNCHED NEXT MONTH
NCP5 J1565 24.1.66.
THERE'S A CERTAIN MAGIC ABOUT HITTING THE TON.
MOTOR CYCLISTS LIVE AND DIE FOR IT. OLD MEN OF
99 PRAY THAT THEY WILL HANG ON FOR THE PRIDE OF
BEING 100 NOT OUT. CRICKETERS' CAREERS RISE AND
FALL BY IT.
BUT NOWHERE IS THE ACHIEVEMENT SO PROUDLY AND
COMPETITIVELY MEASURED TODAY THAN IN SHIPBUILDING.
BUILD A SHIP OF 100,000 TONS OR MORE AND YOU CAN
SAY YOU ARE IN THE BIG LEAGUE, EVEN BY JAPAN'S
GIGANTIC STANDARD. NOW, THE TOUGH, TRADITIONAL
SHIPBUILDERS OF THE RIVER TYNE ARE PUTTING THE
FINISHING TOUCHES TO THEIR FANFARE ENTRY INTO
THE 'BIG LEAGUE.'
A THOUSAND MEN AT THE WORLD-FAMOUS YARD OF
SWAN, HUNTER AND WIGHAM RICHARDSON, WALLSEND-ON-TYNE, ARE SCURRYING OVER AND BELOW THE GIGANTIC
DECKS OF THE 100,000-TON 'BRITISH ARGOSY'
GETTING HER READY FOR LAUNCHING ON FEBRUARY 7TH.
THE VESSEL IS BEING BUILT FOR THE BP TANKER
COMPANY. SHE WILL BE THE FIRST BRITISH-BUILT
SHIP TO ENTER 'BIG LEAGUE' THIS YEAR AND IS THE
BIGGEST SHIP EVER BUILT ON A RIVER RENOWNED FOR
PUSHING THE BOAT OUT IN A BIG WAY.
FIFTEEN YEARS AGO, PRINCESS MARGARET WENT TO
SWAN HUNTERS TO LAUNCH THE THEN BIGGEST SUPER
TANKER OF THE DAY, THE 28,000 TON 'VELUTINA'.
THE BRITISH ARGOSY MAKES THAT LOOK LIKE A ROWING
BOAT. SHE STANDS LIKE AN ENDLESS STRETCH OF
ELASTIC 917FT. LONG, 128FT. WIDE AND 66FT. DEEP,
WITH ENOUGH ROOM ON HER DECKS TO SWALLOW UP NEARLY
THREE FOOTBALL PITCHES.
EVERY SINGLE PIECE OF DRAG CHAIN ON THE WHOLE
OF THE RIVER TYNE, 1 250 TONS OF IT, IS BEING
BEGGED AND BORROWED TO CONTROL HER GRAND SLAM
ENTRY INTO THE RIVER WHEN LAUNCHED BY LADY
BRIDGEMAN (WIFE OF SIR MAURICE BRIDGEMAN, CHAIRMAN
OF BP). EVEN THEN SHE WILL HAVE ONLY 25 YARDS -
LITTLE MORE THAN A CRICKET PITCH LENGTH - IN WHICH
TO AVOID HITTING THE RIVER'S OPPOSITE BANK.
THE BRITISH ARGOSY WILL BE ONLY THE SECOND
BRITISH SHIP OF 100,000 TONS TO BE LAUNCHED TO
DATE. HER SISTER SHIP, BRITISH ADMIRAL, WAS
LAUNCHED FROM VICKERS-ARMSTRONG'S BARROW YARD LAST
YEAR BY THE QUEEN.
PHOTO SHOWS: AN AERIAL VIEW OF THE GIGANTIC
"BRITISH ARGOSY" (100,000 TONS D.W.) WHICH WILL
BE LAUNCHED ON FEBRUARY 7TH.

THE CRICKET BAT HARVEST.         CH/LB

Cricket bat willows, a special tree which is cultivated only
for their manufacture are now being harvested at Witham, Essex,
where hundreds of acres of land are devoted to growing these
trees by Captain Brice, the famous Waterloo Cup judge and an
authority on greyhounds. The trees take from 12 to 15 years
to mature and are worth £15 each, yielding an average of 20
bats per tree.

Photo shows:- Two perfect logs weighing three cwt. make an
awkward but valuable load in transit to the seasoning yards.
Fox Feb 1st. 36.

te.text:
SOUTH WALES.    AW/RI
LOCUSTS MAKE MORE WORK FOR WELSH INDUSTRY.
Plagues of locusts in South America are being fought with a
new idea, incorporating Welsh tinplate. Before the locusts
gain the stage in which they can fly, their only means of
transport is to hop. A barrier of hundreds of miles of sheet
tin, manufactured at Llanelly, is to be built, in front of
which will be a deep trench in which it is hoped to trap the
locusts. The slippery tinplate barrier will prevent them from
getting out, and men with flame throwers can effectively destroy
them.
Photo shows-    Sheets of tinplate coming out of the [illegible]
galvanizing machine at the Llanelly factory.
Fox July 29th. 36.

te.text:
DURHAM PRODUCES DOLLAR-SAVING PIPELINE       D/TAE

One of the biggest contracts for large diamter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teeside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.
(an associate of the Iraq Petroleum Company) is for the
manufacture of 80 miles of 24-inch pipe, weighing 17,000
tons, to be laid next year from the Zubair oilfields in
Southern Iraq to the port of Fao, on the Persian Gulf
near Basrah. In addition to opening new and increasing
markets for the British steel industry, the £900,000
order will mean a saving of some 2 1/2 million dollars, as
hitherto most large diamter oil piping has been obtained
from the United States.

PHOTO SHOWS: A workman at the South Durham Steel and
Iron Company's works, seen grinding the inside seam of
the weld 6" back, as required for pipe laying.

10th June, 1952

activity: Signor Massa, Labour Attache at the Italian Embassy, speaking to miner trainees at Maltby regarding the National Coal Board's decision to suspend recruiting Italian labour.

te.text:
Some will
go home
THE recruiting of Itali-
an labour for
the mines has
been suspended.
Men already
here and not
placed in jobs
will be repatri-
ated by the
National Coal
Board if they
wish to go
home.
The NCB
announced this
yesterday, and
said that Board
officials and
Italian Govern-
ment represen-
tatives were seeing the men to
explain the position.
In the picture above Signor
Massa, Labour Attache at the
Italian Embassy, is telling miner
trainees at Maltby, Yorks, of the
Coal Board's decision.
The Board said that the scheme,
which began last year, had re-
sulted in about 1,200 men being
taken into the pits. About 1,000
more had been brought here and
were in training centres.
For some months there had been
increasing difficulty in placing
Italians, owing to the unwilling-
ness of miners' lodges to accept
them.
The NCB was trying to over-
come the objections, but for the
time being there were few places
open to Italians.
The 31 Italians who were sus-
pended from underground work at
Bullcroft Colliery, near Doncaster,
several weeks ago will not be re-
instated, but will be treated in the
same way as others who cannot
be placed in the mining industry.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
16 MAY 1952
PLEASE RETURN
ART LIBRARY

activity: A view of Bewley Buildings and Dellow Buildings on Cable Street, Stepney, highlighting modernisation of London County Council flats.

te.text:
MODERNISING LCC FLATS. 					PCR/HT.

The London County Council has a programme for the
modernisation of its pre-1919 blocks of flats, and
this morning the Chairman of its Housing Committee,
Mr. W.G. Fiske, held a press conference on the sub-
ject, and those attending went along to the East
End to view some of the achievements of the scheme.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:     A view of Bewley Buildings,
Cable Street, Stepney, a pre-1919 block of LCC
flats, which has been internally renovated with
modern bathrooms, improved kitchens, etc.  To the
left stands another block, Dellow Buildings, which

te.text:
"NYLONS BY THE MILLIONS"
NEW BRITISH FACTORY IS EVERY GIRL'S DREAM    DG/M3

Ten thousand nylon stockings each day, or enough
samples of sheer leg appeal to last a girl a lifetime
if she threw away her stockings every Friday night,
is the target of a high speed modern factory which has
just been opened at Enniskillen, Northern Ireland.
The factory is the result of a combination of
English, Irish, American and Canadian enterprise. It is
equipped with the latest American knitting machines,
though the operatives are mainly Co. Fermanagh
men and women. Fermanagh girls are reputed to
be the most beautiful in the United Kingdom.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "No leg to stand on". Folks who
say there's a shortage should see these gleaming
nylons drying on heated moulds after dyeing,
at the new factory in Enniskillen. Most
of these are, however for export.

activity: aftermath of a fire and explosion at the Ironbridge Metal Company works in Madeley

te.text:
MYSTERY BLAST
KILLS TWO
HERALD REPORTER
IRONBRIDGE, Shropshire, Friday.
A MANAGING DIRECTOR and a woman employee are
believed to have perished in a mystery explosion which
blew the roof off a metal works at Madeley today.
Thirteen others—five women employees and firemen—were
injured.
The three-storeys factory of the
Ironbridge Metal Company was
destroyed by fire.
It was engaged in smelting down
aluminium foil dropped by the
RAF to upset enemy radar—the
stuff German children called
angel's hair.
Families evacuated
More than 100 firemen are
standing by tonight, unable to use
water for fear of causing thermite
in the factory to explode.
They are concentrating on pre-
venting the blaze from spreading
to near-by cottages, from which
families have been evacuated.
Soldiers and firemen had to stop
work about midnight because of
the threat of another explosion.
Clouds of black smoke from the
building indicated that a diesel oil
tank had caught fire.
It was only tonight, after the
police had checked names of
injured at scattered hospitals,
that it was discovered that Mrs.
Kate Healey, of Ironbridge, had
apparently been trapped.
The managing director
is Mr. Ferdinand Fraenkel, who
was an Austrian refugee.
Blitz-like blaze
Troops called out to assist
firemen search the burning
debris after the metal works
explosion yesterday.

activity: A residential building (Housing Flats) where a fatal accident occurred involving a child, Eugene O'Toole.

te.text:
Secret 
dread of 
a proud 
mother 
Herald Reporter 
LITTLE Eugene was 18 
months old, the youngest 
of the five strapping O'Toole 
brothers. A fine, strong 
baby. 
Other mothers smiled enviably 
when Mrs. Ann O'Toole told 
them: "He weighs 35½lb. al- 
ready." But Mrs. O'Toole was 
nagged by a secret dread. 
For when she took him out to 
Wandsworth Common little 
Eugene would play for hours 
and not be tired. Dad used to 
get tired first. 
Shoes? He took size seven. And 
last Saturday Mrs. O'Toole 
bought him two new shirts - 
meant for a boy of three. 
She was proud—yet afraid. And 
yesterday her fear materialised. 
A climb 
Eugene dragged a heavy chair on 
to the balcony of their fourth- 
storey flat in St. Ives House, 
East Hill Estate, Wandsworth, 
and climbed on it. 
Then mothers in the flats opposite 
screamed as he plunged 50ft. to 
the concrete below. He died in 
hospital. 
Last night, 40-year-old Mrs. 
O'Toole, whose other sons are 
aged nine to 21, said: "He was 
so strong, I always feared he 
might do something like that 
when I was not looking. 
I was in another room for only 
second or two. 
He was such a fine baby . . . but 
feel he was sent to break our 
hearts."

DAILY HERALD 
Photograph 
BY L. GARNADE 
NUMBER...1957.728-1

PROPERTY OF 
DAILY HERALD 
- 4 JUN 1957 
PLEASE RETURN 
TO 
ART LIBRARY

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 5TH FEBRUARY 1965.

BRITAIN'S TWO-SLIPWAY GIANT ALMOST
READY FOR LAUNCHING BY QUEEN.
ERF. H. 2090 3RD FEBRUARY 1965.
THE LARGEST VESSEL EVER BUILT IN EUROPE, BRITAIN'S
FIRST 100,000 TON TANKER, TO BE NAMED "BRITISH
ADMIRAL", WILL BE LAUNCHED ON MARCH 17TH BY
THE QUEEN.
THE HUGE TANKER IS BEING BUILT FOR
BRITISH PETROLEUM AT THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONG YARD
AT BARROW-IN-FURNESS, AND IS NOW NEARING COMPLETION.
IT IS THE FIRST OF TWO 100,000 TON DEADWEIGHT TANKERS
BEING BUILT FOR THE B.P. TANKER COMPANY - THE SECOND
IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION AT SWAN HUNTER AND WIGHAM
RICHARDSON YARD ON THE TYNE.
SO GREAT IS THE SIZE OF THE NEW TANKER - IT
WILL BE 917 FT 6 INCHES LONG AND 180 FT IN BREADTH -
THAT TWO BERTHS, EACH 100 FT WIDE WERE RE-BUILT INTO
A SINGLE BERTH TO ACCOMMODATE THE VESSEL. ALL
THE MACHINERY WILL BE INSTALLED COMPLETE PRIOR TO
THE LAUNCHING AND IT WILL BE THE GREATEST-EVER
LAUNCHING WEIGHT AT BARROW. AFTER IT ENTERS THE
WATER, ONLY A FEW WEEKS WILL BE REQUIRED TO PREPARE
THE "BRITISH ADMIRAL" FOR FINAL TRIALS.
PHOTO SHOWS:
A STRIKING AERIAL VIEW OF THE HUGE
B.P. TANKER "BRITISH ADMIRAL", ACCOMMODATING TWO
BERTHS AT THE BARROW-IN-FURNESS YARD OF VICKERS-
ARMSTRONGS, DEPICTING THE HUGE LENGTH AND BREADTH
OF THE 100,000 TON TANKER.

ISSUED BY
FLEET PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
6 & 7, GOUGH SQUARE,
FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4.
FLEET STREET 2266/7

te.text:
FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S DAILIES. JULY 27th. 1954.

UNDER SEA SEARCH FOR OIL.

Commander J.Y. COUSTEAU, famous under-water "explorer"
and author of "Silent World" (he is the greatest living
authority on modern deep-sea diving without heavy diving
suits), has been commissioned by the D'Arcy Exploration
Company, the prospecting subsidiary of the Anglo-Iranian
Oil Company, to investigate the waters off the ABU DHABI
in the Persian Gulf where D'Arcy Exploration Company hold
a concession over 12,000 square miles for a period of 65
years. Commander Cousteau with his team of divers operating
from the research vessel "CALYPSO" will examine the sea-bed
in waters up to 250 feet in depth and bring to the surface
specimens for checking by the Company's geologists on board
the "Calypso". When the result of the survey is assessed
structures worthy of further detailed examination will be
identified with a view to subsequent test drilling.
This picture shows

Two divers about to descend in a shark-proof
cage in the Abu Dhabi marine survey. This
cage is used to hold equipment for the divers
and samples collected. xxxxxxxxpicturexxxxx

te.text:
FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S DAILIES 13.5.46.

THREE IN FOUR NEW BRITISH LOCOMOTIVES GO OVERSEAS

Seventy-five per cent of the output of new locomotives by the
North British Locomotive Company of Glasgow is going overseas.
Current orders include 150 for S.Africa, 110 for India and 40
for Malaya; orders for the home market include 100 for the LNER
as part of a larger consignment. Six years of practically no
replacements enable the works to look forward to a long period
of activity, and in view of the pressure of work the firm is to
recruit several hundred apprentices. The picture shows:
A general view of the erecting shops showing a relatively
small number of locomotives under construction for India,
South Africa and other overseas railways.

activity: a striking view of the "mock-up" (a full size model in wood and brown paper) of the new air liner F.C.I

te.text:
SUB-STRATOSPHERE PLANE.    WS/PAR
THE NEW AIR LINER " F.C.I ".

Following an invitation from the Air Ministry to build a large
fast air liner capable of flying non-stop to any European
capital, the Fairey Aviation Company have designed a four-
engined sub-stratosphere plane of 19 tons with a maximum
speed of 275 m.p.h. fully loaded, and with an air-conditioned
cabin. The plane has a retractable tricycle undercarriage and
a new retractable auxiliary wing. These striking pictures show
the "mock-up" ( a full size model in wood and brown paper ) of
the new air liner F.C.I at the Fairey Aviation factory at Hayes,
Middlesex.

Photo shows- A striking view of the "mock-up" of the F.C.I.
FOX. JULY 6th.39.

PENNY-SIZE DIAMOND AUCTION AT SOTHEBY'S.
This 78 1/2 carat diamond was for sale at Sotheby's today

NOT EVEN £145,000

ONE of the world's
finest diamonds
went up for sale yester-
day.
And it fetched a fine bid—
£145,000, more than three
times the highest price paid
for a diamond in a saleroom.
But it wasn't enough for the
owner, Victor Lyon, 85-year-old
Swiss banking millionaire.
He shook his head slowly to
the auctioneer at Sotheby's,
Frederick Rose, and the dia-
mond was withdrawn from the
sale.
The diamond is large, 78 1/2
carats, about an inch long, and
flawless. Once it belonged to
the Austrian Archduke Joseph
Francis.
Lyon bought it from him in
1936—secretly. Only yesterday
was he identified as the owner.
The bidding started at £50,000
... £4,000 more than the record
price paid for a pink diamond
at Sotheby's last year.
Within seconds two inter-
national diamond dealers,
Harry Winston, of New York,
and Henri Reza, of Paris, had
pushed the bidding up to
£100,000.

won by Manna.

"BOTTLED SUNSHINE"
MATURES FOR CHRISTMAS

DG/ VIG

Row on row of black and cobwebby wine bottle, lies
beneath the main street of the Cambridgeshire town
of Wisbech. Overhead the cars and buses rattle,
but in the firm of Tidnam and Company's
vaults, thousands of bottles of wine are waiting

once ran from Wisbech Castle to the town centre.

of choice wine, in the vaults below the town.
Gunpowder plotters Catesby and Tresham were once

3011 POTTERS' CLAY FROM THE FIELD THAT GROWS

A never-ending supply of clay for the Ewenny Pottery,
near Bridgend, Glamorgan, is obtained from a nearby
field. As fast as the workmen dig out the clay it is
replaced by some natural means. The Ewenny Pottery
was established in 1610 and has been in the Jenkins
family since that time. It is thought to be the oldest
pottery in Wales.

Photo shows :- Mr. Jenkins, proprietor of the Ewenny
Pottery, at the pottery wheel.

present owner at the wheel. On
the left, the clay is being dug
from a field near the works.

WELSH/WEST OF ENGLAND
USED -9 FEB 1939

BUILDING THEMSELVES TO HOMES
Ruislip, Middlesex: Because they were tired of waiting
for homes, 30 young men and their wives of South
Ruislip, got together and decided they would build their
own.
After forming themselves into a 'self-help building group'
they began to practice the technique of laying bricks
while waiting for negotiations with the council over a
building site to be approved. At week ends the group
meets at the home of their 66-year-old president, Councillor
Walter Matthews, where they practice and listen to
lectures by expert workmen.
Next month the self-help builders plan to start putting up
the first house.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The wives join their husbands at brick-laying.
Busy at work are Mr and Mrs Kenneth Isgay, Mr Kingsley Hone
and his wife Josephine, Mr Alan Penfold and wife Vera,
Mr Victor Norman and wife Edith (left to right).

te.text:
BLACKSMITH HOPING FOR A "HAT TRICK".                MJH/FM.

Brawny blacksmith Mr. Jack Pomfrey of London Colney
(Herts) is preparing to defend the London District
Challenge Shield for shoeing horses, during the
competition taking place at the Rural Industries
Vocational Training Centre, Wimbledon on September 3rd.
This contest is open to all blacksmiths within a 30-mile
radius of Charing Cross and Mr. Pomfrey, a 63-years-old
grandfather, has a special incentive for taking his training
very seriously, for he has already won the trophy two years
running and is naturally hoping to perform the "hat trick"
by winning again this year.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: 63-years-old MR. JACK POMFREY of
London Colney (Herts) showing two interested young
visitors to his forge, MOLLY INMAN (12) and RICHARD LUND (10),

A man said to be John Morton, a member of the Holborn (London)
Communist Party, was taken in charge by police after having been
twice warned outside the Ivanhoe Hotel, Bloomsbury Street, London,
where squatters are being blockaded by police.
The man had been telling the squatters the result of a meeting
with Ministry of Works officials.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The man being marched away by police officers.
LUD September 12th 1946 PN.r.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: A large Burmese ruby set in a platinum ring being shown on a lady's hand, accompanied by diamond bracelets.

te.text:
A ruby worth £16,000.  A Burmese ruby three-
quarters of an inch long is being shown by
Wilson and Gill, Regent's Street jewellers.
Weight for weight it is three times as valuable
as the most expensive diamond.  It is price at
over £1,000 a carat.
Apart from real pearls rubies are today the
scarcest of precious gemes and there are only
about six other rubies of equal size and
quality in existence.  A London jeweller
described the stone today as "the Koh-i-Noor
of the ruby world."
The ruby is set in a platinum ring and is
flanked on each side by a single baguette
diamond.  It is square-cut and the surface
of the gem is facetted to display its rich
colour.
0.P.S.            lady's
The ring on a lady's hand, to give some idea
of the size of the ruby, on her wrist is a
thousand pound diamond bracelet and another
small diamond bracelet with a ruby c entre.
This centre ruby although a fine specimen,
is only worth £500.

te.text:
ENGLISH ORANGE CROP                   D/W.11.

Mr. S. Ware of Bigfrith Nursery, Cookham Dean, near
Maidenhead began growing oranges some 14 years ago when
a customer to whom he had supplied an orange tree returned
it because it had grown to large for the conservatory. The
fruit, which takes 15 months to ripen from the arrival of
the blossom, as compared with 9 months abroad, is paler
in colour than normal. It is used for marmalade, being of
the Seville variety, and friends tell Mr. Ware that they
prefer it to imported fruit for the purpose.

PHOTO SHOWS: Mr. Ware's assistant, Miss W. Steer, photo-
graphed tending one of the orange trees at Bigfrith Nursery.
The tree is the largest, is 20 years old, and its best crop
was 150 oranges.

te.text:
Press Information
For Immediate Release

Issued on behalf of JACK OLDING & COMPANY LIMITED

To: News Editors
Trade Press Editors
Industrial Correspondents and
London Correspondents of Overseas Press

NEW VICKERS TRACK-TYPE TRACTOR

180 H.P. Rolls-Royce Engine

Revolutionary Operating Speed

JACK OLDING & COMPANY LIMITED - sole world distributors of the
new Vickers heavy track-type tractor, Model VR 180 - are now able
to release the specification details of this model.

Comparison of its specification with those of other competitive
machines shows that, although its dimensions and weight are no greater,
the VR 180 is considerably more powerful than currently available
tractors.

It sets new standards in tractor operating speed, considerably
reducing the time at present required to move a given quantity of
earth.

A greatly improved suspension technique permits this speed to be
used to the best advantage over rough ground without additional strain
on the driver or increased maintenance cost in respect of the machine.

For detailed specification see overleaf:

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 1 - SEP 1950
PLEASE RETURN
TO

activity: explosion on the Hewitt A drilling platform in the North Sea

te.text:
UPI      LONDON BUREAU

GAS RIG BLOWS UP

IN THE NORTH SEA:  A January 1968 File Photo of
the Gas Rig in the North Sea on which an explosion
occurred on a drilling platform today.  Sixteen men
were plucked from the gale-torn North Sea, and two
more are missing.   Seconds after the explosion the
Rig's standby boat capsized and sank.  Of the survivors
so far recovered 10 are from the gas drilling rig.
A massive hunt - at least six helicopters, two lifeboats
backed up by trawlers and ships in the area - for
the two missing men is still going on.  First to
reach the disaster area and pick up survivors was
the trawler Boston Hornet.  It is understood
40 men were aboard the drilling rig.  The Phillips
Arpet drilling platform Hewitt A,  is 20 miles
off the coast of Norfolk, opposite Cromer.  When
fully developed, it is expected to produce 600
million cubic feet of gas a day.

15th November, 1968 PN-DF
(FILE PHOTO)

UNITED PRESS INTERNATIONAL.

PLANET NEWS,
8, BOUVERIE STREET,
LONDON, E.C.4.
PHONE:- FLE. 3871/2/3.

HEWITT A

te.text:
MR. NUTT BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE 
 September 5th 1963 PAR 105014-2 (PNR/P-R) 
 MR. NUTT BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE 
 Mr. RAYMOND NUTT, a 35-year-old Council house 
 tenant, is seen tiling the roof of the 
 nine-room house he is building at Keynsham, 
 Somerset, for himself and his family and 
 which is now nearing completion. 
 After spending two years on the foundations 
 and drainage, Mr. Nutt started to build last 
 Christmas and pressed on with the job despite 
 the Arctic winter. 
 He has carried out most of the work, 
 doing it in the evenings and at weekends when 
 not at his job on the maintenance staff of a 
 Bristol firm, but he has had help from his wife 
 Margaret and children (a girl and two boys 
 aged 10, 8 and 6), his two brothers and friends. 
 The house, a dormer bungalow built in 
 reconstructed Bath stone with timbered 
 eaves, will be a housewife's dream with 'all 
 mod. cons.' - full central heating (done by 
 a specialist firm), a playroom in the basement 
 for the children, a 'laundrette' off the 
 kitchen-diner and wash basins in the bedrooms. 
 Mr. Nutt reckons it will be worth £4,500. 
 September 5th 1963 PAR 105014-2 (PNR/P-R) 
 FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING 
 PAPERS OF FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 6th.

PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 7 SEP 1963

te.text:
FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S MORNINGS   24.1.50.

WATER INTO "JUICE" WILL TRANSFORM THE HIGHLANDS

The £80 million Hydro-Electric Scheme which will increase
by half the present electricity consumption of the whole of
Scotland and change the face of the Highlands by establishing
new industries andbringing new life to old ones, has made such
progress that this month the first turbine is expected to be
operating in the Loch Sloy Group, thirty miles from Glasgow.
This latest seriesof photographs shows not only the
progress made on the building of the damand the laying of the
giant conduit pipes, but how the electrical part of the vast
project is taking shape. In short, for the first time is shown
the means by which man turns the power of water into that of
electricity and takesit where he wills.  The picture shows a
view looking down the pipe lines (7ft in diameter) leading
from the 2-mile long tunnel under BEN VORLICH to the power
station at INVERRGLAS on the shores of LOCH LOMOND.  The
generating plant at the station will consist of four turbines
driving alternators of 32,500 kw each, and a 450kw Pelton wheel
for auxiliary purposes. The annual output is estimated at
120,000,000 units.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4
CENTRAL 2266/7.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
24 JAN 1950
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

te.text:
HEAPS OF 'LUCK' FOR THE FLAT!
February 27th 1960 PAR 82246-1 (PNR-R)
_________________________________________________
HEAPS OF 'LUCK' FOR THE FLAT!
If horseshoes are true symbols of
good fortune, there are few worries
ahead of racehorse plater DICK CULPIN,
pictured in his Nottingham workshop
where, in readiness for the flat-racing
season, he is busy making the light
alloy plates that are worn by horses
only when they are racing.
One of the few men in the business,
Dick supplies plates to many trainers
in this country (the Queen's trainer
among them) and also sends his products
to many countries overseas, including
Australia, India, Panama, Egypt and
Spain.
February 27th 1960 PAR 82246-1 (PNR-R)
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF MONDAY, FEBRUARY 29th.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
1 - MAR 1960
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: Jacob Halliday, an 82-year-old cobbler known as 'Jolly Jacob', cobbling shoes in his shop and walking with children in Blakeney, Norfolk.

te.text:
Esten.                D.H.            5.1.45.
Jolly Jacob is the Pied Piper of Blakeney.
82 year old Jacob Halliday of Blakeney, Norfolk,
(pop. 662) has repaired the shoes of the children of
this tiny village for the past 66 years without a day off
for illness.  Jacob is known to the rest of the
villagers as "Jolly Jacob" for never lacking a smile.
His shop is always the centre of attraction for the
children who with their faces pressed hard to the
window watch Jacob cobbling and cracking jokes, through
the window panes.
Taking his daily walk around the village he is always
accompanied by a bunch of happy smiling children.
Rising at 5.30 a.m. he works until 8.45. p.m. To his
long beard he attributes the fact that he never catches
cold.  No razor has ever passed over his face.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fuel & Power - Coal, Accidents, Silverwood Colliery near Rotherham, Yorkshire, February 1966

date_info.rationale: Press indexing code '.Fe 1966' indicates the month of publication or filing.

activity: survivors leaving the pit following a coal mine accident

te.text:
DIANE ADSETTS, tall and slim, became a heroine yesterday half-a-mile below ground in the black dust of a coal mine.
By the light of miners’ cap lamps, she worked to save the lives of five men seriously injured in a pit accident.
Nine men were killed in the accident when one pit train rammed another taking 40 men to the pit face.
SHAMBLES
Thirty-one men were injured. The five serious cases included Jack Nettleship, who had both legs cut off in the crash.
Miss Adsetts, aged 38, is a nursing sister at Silverwood Colliery, near Rotherham, Yorks., the pit where the accident happened.
She was on her way to work when the trains crashed.
As the first dust-covered survivors staggered from the pit, she organised first-aid operations.
Then, dressed in red slacks, a green shirt and a miner’s helmet, she went below ground to the injured.
FOUR HOURS
She said later: “I saw the man whose legs had been amputated in the crash.
“He was still conscious and asked for morphine. I put on a tourniquet and splints.
“It was a shambles down there, completely indescribable. Men were lying all over the place. But there was no panic.
“I lost my cap lamp. I don’t know how. When I wanted a light I just grabbed a man and told him to shine his light where I needed it.”
Miss Adsetts, who has worked at the pit for four years, spent nearly four hours underground. Later she was joined by two nursing sisters from neighbouring collieries.
Sister Kathleen Payne, aged 28, of Denaby Colliery, and 47-year-old Sister Mary Parton, of Manvers Main Colliery, helped to get the dead and injured from the pit.
Father of seven Luke Brennan was travelling in one of the crash trains when it was hit from behind by the other, pulled by a 15-ton diesel locomotive.
He said: “Suddenly there was a terrific crash and we were all thrown in the air by the impact.
MARVELLOUS
“Men were trapped and bleeding. Two of my best mates died. Sister Adsetts and the other girls were marvellous. The only wonder is that no more men died.”
Said miner Ernest Devine: “The crash scene was the worst thing I had seen down a pit. It was no place for the squeamish.”
The accident brought tragedy for the second time in the life of 61-year-old Mrs. Lottie Hanton.
Thirty-eight years ago she was made a widow when her first husband died in a pit accident. Yesterday her second husband Jim, aged 59, was killed in the crash.
Last night as survivors praised Miss Adsetts for her work, she said of them: “I thought they acted marvellously. Some had already begun to give first-aid before I arrived.”

te.text:
THE ANCIENT CRAFT OF LACE MAKING 
 RETURNS TO SURREY VILLAGES         DG/RS 
 
 Thanks to the work of MRS H. B. GOAD of Sutton 
 the ancient craft of lace making has been brought 
 to the towns and villages of Surrey, MRS GOAD 
 instructs classes in lace making for the Surrey 
 County Council, and she is one of the few teachers 
 of the craft in the country. Before taking the post 
 18 months ago, she searched antique shops for the 
 old fashioned bobbins needed in the delicate work. 
 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- "Bobbin up again". Some of these 
 inscribed bobbins, seen with Mrs GOAD'S hands 
 on a lace pillow, are hundreds of years old 
 and have been hidden away in antique shops 
 and bureaus drawers. The design is an old 
 Bedfordshire traditional one. Mrs Goads' ancestors 
 made lace for generations at Podington, Beds. 
 FOX PHOTOS April 25th 1950 424873

PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RCD 26 APR 1950 
 PLEASE RETURN

'YOUNG ONES' PROTEST

ELIZABETH THOMPSON
(above) was one of 100
teenagers who marched one
and a half miles through
Kirkby, near Liverpool, yes-
terday chanting: "We want
work."

They are some of more than
400 young people at Kirkby who
cannot find jobs. Their march
was planned to catch the atten-
tion of executives from the
dozens of big factories on Kirk-
by's industrial estate.

They sang The Young Ones—
the pop hit which includes the
words "we may not be the
young ones very long."

The labour situation on Mer-
seyside is sending young people
away to jobs far from home.

Said 20-year-old Vincent
Moore, of Bewley-drive, South-
dene, Kirkby: "I have been to
London twice for a job without
success. In the five years since
I left school I have only worked
for about two and a half. I am
fed up."

from Herald 27th

A "WEIGHTY" JOB, THIS.
WIMBLEDON MUST HAVE PERFECT TENNIS BALLS.

With all the care due to such important
items in the world's most important tennis
tournament, the balls which will be used
at Wimbledon are being made and tested at a
London factory. After the processes of
manufacture have been completed, the balls
are weighed to make sure that they are correct
to the smallest fraction of an ounce,
and then tested for resilience. Those
which do not come up to the required
standard are marked out for a less exalted
future in club or park tennis.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Weighing tennis balls at
the factory.
DRH April 23rd 1935 PN.r.

nance.

veyors, all operated by remote
control.
Closed circuit TV cameras will
replace the human eye to watch
for unforeseen defects like a

perly.

achieved next year, 770 men will
mine 1 1/2 million tons a year. This
is equal to an output per man per
shift of 160 cwts. - nearly five
times as much as in the aver-
age mine.

te.text:
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE SATURDAY, DEC. 17th.

16.12.60.
PREVIEW OF BRANDON ESTATE, SOUTHWARK.
TO BE OPENED TOMORROW.

Brandon Estate, Southwark, a major
L.C.C. project combining the rehabilitation of nearly
200 old houses with the provision of over 1,000 new
dwellings ranging from old persons' bungalows to 18-
storey point blocks, will be opened tomorrow (Dec 17),
by the Chairman of the L.C.C. (Mrs. F.E. Cayford).
The estate is one of the largest of the L.C.C.'s
redevelopment schemes for inner London, and is the
first example of the L.C.C.'s policy of infusing new
life into decaying areas of London's "middle belt" by
combining the complete redevelopment of the property
in worst condition with thorough modernisation of
property still in sound structural order. There is
accommodation for 5,000 people, and the estimated
total cost of the work is £3,596,450.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- 68-year old FRANK WEAVER,
seen in his Old People's bungalow, on the
estate - at today's preview.
H/Keystone BM/725098
Housing - Flats, and New Estates. (SEE ALSO - LONDON - SOUTHWARK)

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 DEC 1960
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: introducing a young Kivu gorilla named Meng to a baby chimpanzee named Jacqueline at the London Zoo

te.text:
SAIDMAN.  10.8.38.
A New Husband for "Moina"
The Belgian Government have presented the London
Zoo with a new husband for "Moina". He isn't
old enough or big enough to go with her yet
as he is only about a year old. "Meng" as he
is called after the village where he was fouhd,
is a sturdy and intelligent little youngster of
the Mountain or Kivu race of Gorilla. When he
grows up he will be almost twice the size of the
late lamented "Mok". Male Kivu Gorillas when
fully grown weigh up to 600 pounds. "Meng"
is being introduced today to "Jacqueline"
the baby Chimpanzee at the Zoo which has been
brought up on the bottle by her keepers. It
is hoped that they will take to each other
and be company for each other until "Meng"
is big enough to be put with "Moina".

The trawler 'Loch Doon', owned by the Walker Steam Trawl Fishing Co. Ltd., Aberdeen, was recently launched from the shipyard of Alexander Hall and Co. Ltd., Aberdeen.

activity: One of the potters using an old-time kick wheel to fashion the lip of a coffee jug.

te.text:
HAND-MADE POTTERY FROM AN ESSEX BRICKFIELD.  AW/TAR

A brickyard which has been worked in the little village
of Bulmer, near Halstead, Essex, for 150 years, is now
suddenly producing pottery which has found its way overseas
to export markets and to the windows of fashionable London
shops.  Recently, a seam of strong clay was uncovered by
the brickmakers.  It proved suitable for making pottery
and slip-ware of high quality which is fired in the kiln
alongside the bricks.  An old outhouse of the brickworks
is being used by two potters, and a girl is modelling
figures from the same clay.  Without the aid of modern
machinery, the potters are producing works of individual
quality which bear the hallmark of the English craftsman.

Photo shows:-  One of the potters using an old-time kick
wheel to fashion the lip of a coffee jug.
Fox Nov 10th. 48.

(below) works on the keel.

activity: A famous Derbyshire geologist making an examination of the quartz veins.

te.text:
144)    REPORTED DISCOVERY OF GOLD IN DERBYSHIRE.

The discovery is reported in a lonely Derbyshire valley,
quite near a main road, yet only a few miles from a busy
population, of a similar quartz to that found in South
African gold mines. Tests have been made with the rock,
which is reported to contain gold in varied amounts. The
discovery was made near one of the many extinct volcanoes
in the valley, and search is now being made to find the
main lode of the quartz, as the place where the find was
made has since proved to be a deposit left by molten lava,
many thousands of years ago. The present position of the
discovery is at present being kept a secret.

Photo shows:- A famous Derbyshire geologist making
an examination of the quartz veins.

te.text:
JS    THE BIGGEST 'WALKING DRAGLINE' IN THE WORLD
                                                    31.10.51.
The world's largest 'walking dragline' - with a jib 282ft
long and a bucket weighing 22 tons and holding 27 tons of
spoil when full - is now working in the ironstone quarries
of Messrs Stewarts and Lloyds at Corby. Constructed by
Ransomes and Rapiers, Ltd it has taken four years to build,
and it walks under its own power with seven-foot steps.
The dragline is now removing the strata covering the
ironstone bed down to a depth of 100 feet, hoisting the
loaded bucket (a dead weight of about 50 tons) to the
top of the quarry and slews round to deposit the spoil.
Although the [strikeout] giant machine weighs 1600 tons, and
in its working position is 5 feet taller than Nelson's
Column, it is controlled entirely by one man.

activity: Mr John Nicol panning for gold specimens in Milehopeburn near the rediscovered lost gold mine of Yarrow.

te.text:
2389)    THE LOST GOLD MINE OF YARROW FOUND.

The Ancient workers closed down their Gold mine and
thoroughly camouflaged the workings until every
particle of Quartz was hidden.
Huge stones were erected to mark the place and a
chart would probably be made. Centuries have
passed and now it has been re-discovered by Mr.
John Nicol of Glen Cafe, St. Marys Loch, Yarrow.
In 1933 an article by a German about mining appeared
in a Canadian paper remarking about the lost Gold
mine of Yarrow. Was this mine worked by foreigners in
lone ages past and information handed down through
the generations.
The Gold is both Alluvial and native(ie. in the Sand
of the streams as well as in Reefs)
Back tracking was first noticed in the HENDERLAND
BURN (Backtracking for alluvial mining) as well as the
COM SIKE but particularly in the MILEHOPEBURN where
extensive sluicing had been carried out at two
distinct periods. The Gold is not free in the Rock
area, it is combined with other Reef Ores including
Manganese Copper, Gold and Silver.
Preliminary samples drawn from decomposed back of
Reef Assays showed 2.4 Dwts of Gold per ton of 2240
lbs or 58 grains to the Ton as well as 0.36 ozs of
silver and also included Manganese and Copper.
St. Mary's Loch is a very well known and beautiful
loch and a great many visitors are to be found there
in peace time. The situation is between Selkirk and
Moffat. It is in Selkirkshire and 18 miles from
Selkirk.

Photo shows: Mr John Nicol of St. Mary's Loch, who
rediscovered the gold mine, panning for specimens
in Milehopeburn, showing a reef uncovered on right
hand side.

20/3/44  Topical Press  (Y.I5436)

FILE INDUSTRY METAL. GOLD
NR. SELKIRKSHIRE V

activity: curing, dressing and plucking coypu pelts to make a fur coat

te.text:
LN 370076 GOU LONDON BUREAU
MAKING A FUR COAT FOR THE WIFE.
GREAT YARMOUTH, NORFOLK : MR. HARRY SMITH OF THREE MILE
HOUSE, NEAR GREAT YARMOUTH IS BUSY CURING, DRESSING AND
PLUCKING SOME FORTY PELTS OF COYPU'S WHICH HE HAS CAUGHT OR
SHOT ON THE MARSHES AROUND HIS HOME OVER THE PAST THREE
YEARS. WITH THESE PELTS, HE INTENDS TO MAKE A COAT FOR HIS
WIFE, FOR THE FUR FROM THE BELLIES OF COYPU, WHEN CURED AND
DRESSED, BECOME NURTIA, USED TO MAKE FUR COATS WHICH CAN
COST UP TO £300. UNFORTUNATELY, IF MR. SMITH HAS HIS COYPU
PELTS MADE PROFESSIONALLY INTO A COAT, THERE IS A MATTER OF
ABOUT 6/- IN THE POUND PURCHASE TAX PAYABLE ON THE VALUE OF
THE SKINS IN ADDITION TO THE COST OF HAVING THE COAT MADE,
WHICH MR. SMITH CONSIDERS A LOT OF MONEY TO PAY IN PURCHASE
TAX ON SOMETHING THAT WAS NOT PURCHASED IN THE FIRST PLACE.
IN THE MEANTIME, MR. SMITH CONTINUES TO PREPARE THE COYPU
PELTS, A TASK REQUIRING MUCH TIME AND PATIENCE.
9TH FEBRUARY, 1959 PN-s

activity: demonstrating a Secura machine for determining the sex of a chick at a Kent County Agricultural Executive Committee poultry conference

te.text:
DETERMINING THE SEX OF A CHICK
There are now three British machines
on the market for determining the sex
of a chick.  Hitherto, poultry farmers
had to rely on the services of a chick
sexing expert (with about 90 - 95%
accuracy) but now unskilled labour after
a little instruction can now sex chicks
without failures.
    The three machines are more or less
similar in operation - being a n
anatomically shaped tube inserted in the
rectum of the chick.  The sight field
of the chick's organs are illuminated by
reflected light, and by magnification,
a view is seen either of the ovaries of
the female or the testicles of the male.
    The machines average about £35
each - while their Japanese counterparts
are well over a hundred pounds.  It
was Japan who commenced the exacting
business of chick sexing, at which they
are real experts.
    These machines were all demonstrated
at a Kent County Agricultural Executive
Cpmmitte (N.A.A.S.) Poultry Conference
at Ashford, Kent, recently.
    (The machine here is a Secura).

activity: Martin Hulme and his mother Mrs. Trudy Hulme in their garden with beanstalks that grew to 16ft from seeds received three years prior.

te.text:
ONCE UPON A TIME a boy got a bag
of beans . . .
Now sit back and stop fidgeting. This
story is true.
The beans were sent to Martin Hulme.
They were attached to a birthday card
from an aunt in Yorkshire on his fifth
birthday.
“These are magic beans from birthday
land,” the printed card told Martin.
“Just plant them, add some water, and
like Jack’s beanstalk, they will grow and
grow and grow!”
Martin planted his beans in the back
garden of his home in England Place,
Congleton, Cheshire, and watered them
every day as the card said in rhyme.
And what do you know? They did
grow and grow.
Now, three years later, the tallest stalk
is 16ft. and still reaching for the sky.
Martin said: “The beanstalk is so strong
I can climb it.”
His mother, Mrs. Trudy Hulme, is
puzzled at the monster in her garden.
“Nothing happened for a year after
Martin planted the beans,” she said.
“Then they really began to shoot up.
We have no idea what the plants are.”
The aunt in Yorkshire cannot explain
it—nor can the firm who printed the
card. “Normally, the beans are runner-
beans,” a spokesman said yesterday.
Mr. Elms, the Herald Gardener, says:
“The species probably comes from
abroad. I know of no English tree that
would grow 16ft. from seed in three
years.”

"SILVER COD" FISH TROPHY

___________________________________________________________________________

The "Silver Cod" trophy, presented annually as a challenge
cup to the British trawler responsible for the heaviest catch of
fish in the year.

activity: tipping coal from lorries on to a portable screen for separation into fines and round coal at Bold Colliery

te.text:
The National Coal Board have begun to lift their coal 
stocks, and already undistributed stocks have been reduced 
by about 1 1/2 million tons from the mid-December peak of 
36.5 million tons.  One of the Board's problems in lifting 
these stocks is to ensure that customers don't suffer as 
a result of any deterioration in the size of the coal during 
stocking. 

One method of overcoming this problem, in use at 
BOLD COLLIERY in Lancashire, is shown in this photograph. 
Coal from stock is tipped from lorries on to a portable 
screen which is fed from the elevator shown in the centre 
of the picture.  The screened coal, separated into fines 
and round coal, is then fed into separate conveyances, 
either the wagons on the right of the picture or lorries 
which are hidden behind the lorry in the foreground. 

N.C.B. Press Office. 
2nd Feb.1960.

activity: 62-year-old William Scudder working on the last pair of boots made by the bespoke bootmakers Peal & Co. Ltd. for the Household Cavalry.

te.text:
KT/RS.

BESPOKE BOOTMAKERS CLOSES DOWN THROUGH LACK OF CRAFTSMEN.

Last week saw the closing down of the World-famous
bespoke bootmakers PEAL & Co.Ltd. of Wigmore Street.
Up to the end the business was still being run by
father and son directors MR.CECIL and MR.RODNEY PEAL,
fifth and sixth generation of the family who founded
the business 174 years ago. Among it's clients, are
EARL MOUNTBATTEN, the DUKE OF WINDSOR, the late SIR
WINSTON CHURCHILL, for whom they made boots and shoes
for 40 years up until his death, and host of Royal and
other prominent personages. Although they have been
getting about 1,000 new clients every year, they are
closing because they just cannot get the skilled
craftsmen essential to maintain their high standard.
Most of the clients had their owns lasts, from which the
shoes were made, measurements being exact to the 
millimetre, and the lasts are now being sold to the
customers for 3 guineas each.

PHOTO SHOWS.
62-year-old MR.WILLIAM SCUDDER of Shepherd's
Bush who has been at PEAL's for 49 years, is seen working
on the last pair of boots that the firm is making, for
the Household Cavalry. PEAL's have been making boots for
the Household Cavalry and Horse Guards, which call for a
high degree of skill, for many years.
FOX PHOTOS			9th FEBRUARY 1965			717384.

Makers of lenses and frames for spectacles are
still trying to cope with the rush of hundreds of
thousands of orders resulting from the National
Health Service. Demands far exceeded expectations
and costs have naturally soared. Indications are
that the figure of 10 million pounds will be passed.

strong.

activity: A barrier of straw bales closing the road to the Crickley Barrow Farm

te.text:
KT/MAE.
FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE PRECAUTIONS.
Except for two cases, Gloucestershire has so far
escaped the current outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease,
but farmers are keeping a close watch on the situation,
and most have laid disinfected straw at the entrances to
their farms. This has been carried out on all roads over
the Stowell Park estate where large numbers of stock are
kept, and roads leading to farms only have been closed to
all non-essential vehicles.
PHOTO SHOWS.
A barrier of straw bales closing the road
to the Crickley Barrow Farm near Northleach, Glos.
Breeding experiments are carried out at the farm, and
any outbreak of disease would be particularly serious.
FOX PHOTOS    27th NOVEMBER 1967    769499.

on May 15th 1962. plastic containers for motor oil. The containers are

te.text:
LEWES GAOL-BREAKER CAUGHT AT LAST.
SHOP ASSISTANT'S FLYING TACKLE.
Stanley Hilton Thurston, the man for whom
every policeman in the country has been
looking since his escape from Lewes Gaol
with another prisoner on August 9, was re-
captured in Oxford Street today after a chase
and a struggle. He was followed into
Attenborough's,the jewellers, in Oxford
Street, whore he tried to pawn a diamond
ring. Seeing the police, he ran out of the
shop, but was caught in Oxford Street by
Leslie Fearse, an assistant in Attenborough's.
O.P.S.
Mr R. A. Ewen & Mr S. Langford who tackled Thurston

CENTURY OF GROWTH OF FAR WESTERN U.S.
FOLLOWED CALIFORNIA GOLD RUSH OF 1849

Settlers of California who rushed west for
gold later discovered that oil was a great and
steady source of wealth in the Pacific coast
state. California now has 26,676 producing oil
and gas wells of which 297 are exclusively gas
wells. The three major oil-producing areas of
the state are in the San Joaquin Valley, the Los
Angeles area and the coastal region. Some of the
wells are drilled offshore into the ocean bottom.
California was second in the United States in
1948 in petroleum yield. The photo shows a scene
that is typical of many highly productive oil
fields in California. (SO-60430)

accompanying text.)

activity: British drilling crews operating on the BP drilling platform 'Sea Gem' in the North Sea, specifically mentioning the communications room.

te.text:
BRITISH DRILLING CREWS MAKE GOOD PROGRESS
ON 'SEA GEM'

'Sea Gem', BP's first drilling platform for the North
Sea oil and gas search spudded in on her location 42 miles East
of the Humber on June 5th.

The 5,600 ton platform was towed to her location by two
tugs with a third smaller one in attendance. After being
positioned precisely between four marker buoys her 10 huge legs
were lowered to the sea bed and the deck jacked up 50 feet above
sea level, out of reach of the largest waves.

Forty men crew "Sea Gem". They work in two shifts, 12
hours on and 12 off for 10 days. A third off-duty crew remains
ashore on five days leave. Two-thirds of the men have had
extensive overseas experience of off-shore drilling with BP and
they are the only all-British drilling crews operating in the
North Sea.

O.P.S. The communications room of "Sea Gem" is crammed full
of equipment, including teleprinters and ship-to-shore
radio.

8177/12 BP Photograph

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
9 JUL 1965
Please return to
ART LIBRARY

activity: molten iron being tapped from cupolas in a Letchworth foundry before conversion into steel

te.text:
A HERTFORDSHIRE STEEL WORKS.

Steel works are usually associated with South Wales or the
Industrial North, but it is a surprising fact that the steel
foundry with the largest output of carbon or plain steel
castings in the country is situated at Letchworth, Herts, only
30 miles from London. It provides employment for 1,500 work-
people, many hundreds of whom have migrated from the North and
distressed areas. The work on hand is for a variety of industries
ranging from ship building and locomotives to power stations and
cigarette machinery. The flow of steel means a flow prosperity
for thousands of homes in Hertfordshire and it is hoped to find
employment for several hundred more by the end of 1937.

Photo shows- A striking scene in the Letchworth foundry showing
molten iron being tapped from cupolas before conversion into
steel. converter can be seen sending up a shower of sparks
in background.
Fox Jan 6th. 37.

COPYRIGHT
FOX PHOTOS LTD
6 TUDOR STREET,
E.C.4.
CENTRAL 7831

activity: Mrs. Gwyneth Davies and her daughter Lynn looking down from their 15th-floor flat in the Brandon Estate as part of a survey on high-rise living.

te.text:
should have been heaven, moving from the squalid back-streets of slumland to bright, skyscraper luxury flats, with their constant hot water and built-in central heating. 
 But many young mothers living in the upper storeys are finding it hell. The reason? "We are tied to our toddlers. We must watch them the whole time. We live in constant dread of them getting out of windows, and falling from the balconies." The ground is 180ft. below. 
 The "high-life" mothers put balconies out of bounds, of course. The doors leading to them are kept locked. But windows cannot be locked. 
 Worry 
 Mesh guards on every balcony are essential. And so are playgrounds or day nurseries for "high-life" under-fives, so that they can make friends and play with children of their own age in safety. 
 These suggestions are made in a report "Two to Five in High Flats," published today — the result of a survey of 200 "high-lifers" by mother-of-three, Mrs. Joan Maizels, with help from the Joseph Rowntree Memorial Trust. 
 Mrs. Maizels found that the higher mothers live, the more they worry about their toddlers' safety. 
 And because of the lack of supervised play space, they are "frightened to turn their backs" on their children. 
 The only outings enjoyed by half of the under-fives covered in the survey are to the shops. Their only playground: the flat. 
 One toddler in seven never played with the children of other families, and the general rule was only "occasional visits" to parks and playgrounds. 
 Mrs. Maizels told me yesterday: "Mothers do realise the importance of play to their children. Play is a most necessary part of a toddler's training. His future character depends on his pre-school years." 
 But — what can the mothers do? 
 A small committee supervised Mrs. Maizel's investigations. One of the members, Mrs. Eirene White, M P (Labour, East Flint), said: "Much more is done for young children in other parts of Europe. We would like to see a lot more supervision of play. I'm sure it's not good for mothers and toddlers to be together all the time." 
 "This report shows that many of them are. For three-quarters of the children under five, living above the fifth storey, are never allowed to play alone anywhere but in the flat — with an anxious mother close at hand. 
 That is exactly what I found at the Brandon Estate, Walworth, London, yesterday, where the flats soar 18 storeys high. 
 Auburn-haired Lynn Davies, nearly two, has no friends of her own age, and has no opportunity of ever playing with other children. Her mother, 24-year-old Mrs. Gwyneth Davies, from Yorkshire, hopes that she can soon take Lynn to a nursery school. "She needs the company of other toddlers. She needs adventure in her play. But not danger, of course."

THERE WERE, at the
latest count, some 120 firms

without any noticeable in-
stant effect on the housing
lists.
This one is a little differ-
ent. It took just six days
to build and furnish which
may well be a record of
sorts.
But the man who, meta-
phorically speaking, built
the £4,000, centrally-heated
house with all mod. con., is
not shouting too loud just
now. 'It's not unique,' 33-
year-old Mr. John Davies,
managing director of Anvil
Enterprises Ltd., modestly
admitted. 'But we think
we have gone further than
anybody.'
Four men put up the
house in two days on an
exhibition site in Hereford,
just to show it could be
done. Then they spent four
days adding the trimmings,
and on the seventh day they
rested, saw that it was good,
and promptly sold it.
The idea is to do for
private buyers what the
other instant builders are
supposed to be doing for the
councils. Now all that re-
mains is the slight problem
of rustling up an instant
mortgage. . .

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
----
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs.May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenites. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T.Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.

activity: a farm labourer examining cut oats sprouting in the stook after being left in bad weather

te.text:
KENT OATS ARE SPROUTING IN THE STOOK
-----
This farm labourer on a farm at Green Street
Green, near Dartford, Kent, is examining cut oats
which have been out in the weather for the past week
or two - unable to be harvested.
Now, with stooks blown about, grain blown from
the shells, the corn is sprouting where it has fallen
on the ground.
A loss there is, though as yet not serious, but
unless the weather changes quickly this farmer, like
several others who cut their corn some weeks ago, will
find their harvest not worth collecting.

activity: the world's largest 'walking dragline' removing strata covering an ironstone bed in a quarry

te.text:
JS THE BIGGEST "WALKING DRAGLINE" IN THE WORLD
31.10.51.
The world's largest "walking dragline" - with a jib 282ft
long and a bucket weighing 22 tons and holding 27 tons of
spoil when full - is now working in the ironstone quarries
of Messrs Stewarts and Lloyds at Corby. Constructed by
Ransomes and Rapiers, Ltd it has taken four years to build,
and it walks under its own power with seven-foot steps.
The dragline is now removing the strata covering the
ironstone bed down to a depth of 100 feet, hoisting the
loaded bucket (a dead weight of about 50 tons) to the
top of the quarry and slews round to deposit the spoil.
Although the [monster] giant machine weighs 1600 tons, and
in its working position is 5 feet taller than Nelson's
Column, it is controlled entirely by one man.

activity: meat hanging in the Cold Storage Commission cold room in Salisbury before being packed

te.text:
F194 | D1 
 Industry food & drink 
 MEAT (inc sausages)

CHILLED BEEF BY AIR 
 HAM.   13.2.59 
 THE FIRST CONSIGNMENT OF CHILLED BEEF EVER TO BE SENT 
 BY AIR FROM CENTRAL AFRICA HAS ARRIVED IN SMITHFIELD 
 FROM SALISBURY, RHODESIA. THE MEAT LEFT SALISBURY 
 ON WEDNESDAY NIGHT AND WAS IN SMITHFIELD LAST NIGHT. 
 THERE WAS [illegible] 1500 POUNDS OF HIND QUARTERS AND IT IS 
 PURELY AN EXPERIMENT TO SEE HOW THE MEAT LASTS ON THE 
 JOURNEY, AND TO FIND OUT IF SUCH A METHOD OF SHIPPING 
 IS POSSIBLE. THE MEAT WAS NOT SPECIALLY SELECTED AND 
 IT WAS ONLY CHILLED TO 28 DEGREES SO THAT THE CONDITION 
 IN WHICH IT ARRIVED IN LONDON WAS BEING WATCHED WITH 
 SPECIAL INTEREST IN RHODESIA. A REGULAR SERVICE OF MEAT 
 BY AIR IS NOT ENVISAGED FOR THE NEAR FUTURE UNLESS VERY 
 CHEAP AIR FREIGHT RATES CAN BE OBTAINED. 
 THE PICTURE SHOWS THE MEAT HANGING IN THE COLD 
 STORAGE COMMISSION COLD ROOM IN SALISBURY BEFORE 
 BEING PACKED.

PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 14 FEB 1959 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO 
 ART LIBRARY

activity: 84-year-old John Beddow watches his colleague Charles Griffiths sign on for the day's work at an 'Old Folks Workshop' for workers over 70.

te.text:
TO WORK with a smile: 84-year-old John Beddow watches one
of his workmates sign on for the day's work.

"SONS OF REST" SIGN ON.

GK/7262-1. John Beddow (left) Aged 84, watches as his mate,
Charles Griffiths, aged 73, signs on at 8.30 a.m. Working day
starts at 8.30 and finishes at 5. The men in the main factory
start at 7.30 a.m. and have to clock in. The old workers
appreciate their extra hour in bed in the morning. They work
a five-day week.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY

GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co, of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
2- MAY 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: Opening and tasting oysters on an oyster dredger in Whitstable

te.text:
220112    DAW

THEY CAME, THEY SAW - THEY TASTED!

Whitstable; Kent:    Oysters - those delectable
little lumps that taste like heaven with a glass
of beer.......And of all the places to taste
them, these men have chosen the one ideal spot -
on an oyster    dredger itself.
The men are buyers, restauranteurs and club- and
oyster-bar owners. They travelled down to
Whitstable, in Kent, to see for themselves just
how the industry is run. They saw the succulent
shell-fish being landed and washed. And of
course they tasted them for themselves.
Opening oysters on the left is Mr. Foreman, of
the Whitstable Oyster Company.
September 20th. 1951. PN-h.

3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
