activity: demonstrating the very latest in metal spraying equipment

te.text:
KT/RS.

THE NEW SPACE LOOK AT WOKING.

      The four with the "space-like" look are in fact
demonstrating the very latest in metal spraying
equipment, produced by the METCO company at Chobham,
Woking. The two men on the left are actual sprayers,
while the girls are secretaries with the firm who are
demonstrating the lightness and comfort of the masks.
The main hood is of lightweight fibre glass with an
easily replaceable clear visor, and the weight is
supported by the body instead of the head, making it
practical for it to be worn for long periods. The usual
smell of stale, oil-bearing compressed air experienced
when spraying has been removed by fitting an activated
carbon filter in the air feed line, and a quick-release
connector allows the line to be disconnected so that
the operator can leave the work area without removing
the mask. The size of the mask allows an unusual degree
of movement, and makes it practical for spectacles to
be worn if necessary.

PHOTO SHOWS.
             Trying the new equipment (left to right)
sprayers CLIFFORD WATERSof Maidenhead and ERNEST
WATTS of Chobham, and secretaries CAROL HOLLAND, 21,
and ROSEMARY SUTTON, 21, both of Chobham.

600 DWELLINGS AT DASHWOOD VILLAGE			MW/MRE

Wycombe & West Wycombe and west of Plomer Hill, it covers

property of West Wycombe. There will be 600 dwellings on

hall. There will be linked, detached, & terraced houses with

house with carport adjoining the next ranch house. Each
have 3 bedrooms and a large living /dining room. It costs
about £6,500, which included carports, garages, patios, full
central heating. It also has gas fired warm air ducted
to each room, with a time clock. Waste disposal kitchen
units, and wired TV.

near future. The aircraft are for use on the Far East

passenger craft fitted with four engines.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fishing, Accidents - Trawler Losses, January/February 1968 - Families, Demonstrations, etc
activity: Bill Howbrigg, cook of the Ross Cleveland, recounting his experience on the trawler during severe icing conditions.

te.text:
THE COOK of the Ross Cleveland, Bill Howbrigg, aged 59, was taken off the ship last Thursday with pneumonia. After treatment at a hospital in Iceland he was flown home to Hull.
Last night he said: "The weather was dreadful. If it had been up to me I would never have taken a trawler fishing up there.
"The weather was so bad that we had only two days' fishing before I had to leave the ship. Every 12 hours we were out smashing the ice which was making the ship top-heavy.
Axes
"We were using axes, batons, spanners—anything we could lay our hands on. But the weight of ice was forcing the ship down. Sometimes it was impossible to go on deck to clear it.
"We would just get one side cleared, the ship would start to right herself—and then the other side would freeze up. It was murder. If you've never seen it, I can't describe it to you. In weather like this it's like a white hell up there."
Bill, who is unmarried, was talking at the Queen Mary hostel where he lives.
Shocked
He said: "I have been on trawlers since 1926. I would say this weather was as bad as that in which the Lorella and Roderigo were lost 13 years ago.
"But if I am passed medically fit I will still go back to sea.
"I did not want to go to hospital, but the skipper made me go ashore.
"I stayed in hospital until last Friday. All I can say is that I am deeply shocked, but, thank God, I was lucky enough to get out alive."

[purple crayon mark, possibly a letter or checkmark]

E.M./RS.

A CORNISH TIN MINE.

The tin-mining industry in Cornwall, so ancient that most
people had forgotten about it, takes on a new importance with
the loss of our supplies from Malaya; however, before it
can be exploited to the full a Government grant would be
necessary. Water has to be pumped away from the mine at
the rate of 1,000 gallons per minute, the mine being 2,000
feet deep. The miners descend in a cage to the bottom of
the mine; they drill holes five or six feet deep and charge
then with explosives - the next shift on duty clears up the
ore and insert fresh charges.

Photo shows:- Coming up from the bottom of the mine,
each shift is glad of a wash before they go home.  269195.
FOX. 2nd February, 1942.

te.text:
VAST MACHINES WILL DRIVE FLOATING METROPOLIS -
PROGRESS ON WORLD'S GREATEST LINER AT CLYDEBANK.

The thousands of tons of machinery necessary to
drive the world's greatest liner, the "Queen Mary",
is being installed at Clydebank, Scotland.
although rapid progress has been made on the liner
since the launch last September, it has mainly
been in connection with the machinery and
auxiliary equipment.
This was necessary because until the enormous
components, some of them weighing as much as 200
tons, had been hoisted on board, the work of
completing the plating of the decks could not proceed.
PHOTO SHOWS: One of the huge turbine-rotors,
weighing many tons, being made ready for the
"Queen Mary" at Clydebank.
AND  March 10th 1935  PN.r.

steel structure for the 300-ft. high chimney

activity: the old coastguard station... being moved lock, stock and chimney pot to its new site

te.text:
PICKED UP any good bargains on the property market lately? One man who has, literally, is Mr. Jack Carmichael, of Long Island, New York.
Our picture shows the old coastguard station he fell in love with being moved lock, stock and chimney pot to its new site.
We in Britain have more ancient buildings to be sentimental about than the Americans, but our hysterical road conditions prevent us from keeping historical buildings intact in this way.
"Streets in the United States are fantastically wide," said a heavy haulage expert at Pickfords.
"Ours are generally so narrow and cluttered by overhead wires that it wouldn't be possible to drive a house through them."
The upper storeys of a 16th-century house were moved last year to be built into a new chain store on the same Hereford site. But the cost was £6,000.
A Cambridgeshire woman had her home dismantled brick by brick to be rebuilt on another site rather than have it bulldozed. This cost £8,000.
Too costly
Costs like these are too high for the average home owner. So the rooms in our homes are doomed to keep their old familiar views.
But in America it is a different story.
The fishing and farming families who live along the far reaches of Eastern Long Island, New York State, would wonder why we find the picture above so remarkable.
For to them, making way for tomorrow without losing yesterday is a commonplace event. There's even a man who "collects" old houses on his shore-line estate and rents them out for the summer.
The coastguard station was going cheap because the land it stood on was needed for a fishing museum.
Mr. Robert Kennelly, who has been moving houses all his working life, explained: "Very often what was once an ideal spot becomes the corner of a new highway or the centre of an industrial complex. Or maybe even some noisy neighbours move in next door.
"So then we get a call to move the house to a new spot. The owner buys a new parcel of land and we move the house for them."
The longest move Mr. Kennelly has done so far has been 60 miles.

HOUSE MOVER
ROBt KENNELLY
WAVES TRUCK
ON WAY TO
NEW LOCATION

PROPERTY
SUN
14 SEP 1966
Please return to
ART LIB-

STEPHENS. CARDIFF.          30/6/55
More than thirty National Coal Board pit
ponies and horses will be on exhibition at
the Royal Show at Nottingham next week,
including six horses from South Wales.
One of these will be 'Ponty', a 13 year
old horse that has been working underground
at Rochin Colliery, Tredegar, Mon, since
1947.
Ponty is the last horse left at Pochin
Colliery, so when he was brought to the
surface ready for this show, 'Ginger' the
stable cat came up too.
Ginger has been going underground for
fourteen years, and is very friendly with Ponty.
Mr. Horse keeper Mr. George Ingles has
Ginger on his shoulder as the cat says her
farewells to Ponty.

activity: The construction of an Orlit pre-fabricated bungalow at a secret site in London during WWII.

te.text:
The guard, to the Orlit House.
see story by Cummings

2-DAY
HOUSE
BUILT
By R. GORDON CUMMINGS
NUMBER EIGHT in the
range of pre-fabricated
bungalows is now going up.
It is the Orlit.
Soon after daybreak yester-
day work began on the Minis-
try of Works secret site behind
the Tate Gallery.
By 1.30 p.m. the framework was
up and everything set to put on
the asbestos roof and fill in the
walls. It will be finished some
time to-day.
When I saw the skeleton yester-
day riveters and drills were
clattering away.
At the far end of the secret
“pen” finishing touches were
being put to the Phoenix, design of
the “Mulberry” men.
In between were two other
models still on the secret list—
the Spooner and Universal.
25,000 A Year
Over the other side of a high
wooden fence people were inspect-
ing the original models, the Arcon,
Tarran, Uni-Seco and Portal
Mark II.
Framework of the Orlit is steel
with concrete posts and steel roof
stanchions. Walls are made from
foam slag inside and stone-faced
concrete slabs outside.
Captain C. Ramsden, managing
director of Orlit, Ltd., told me
that production can begin in a
very short time. “I have offered
to turn out 25,000 in 12 months,”
he said.
Late last night lights were burn-
ing in a big office suite in Victoria.
The “Mulberry” men were mak-
ing last-minute changes in the
Phoenix, which the Government
has just adopted.

Daily Herald
Copyright
Photograph.
Number ...

activity: Princess Elizabeth laying the foundation stone of a new church in Bromley to replace one destroyed in 1941.

te.text:
190146    GAI

PRINCESS ELIZABETH LAYS FOUNDATION OF A NEW CHURCH -
         TO RISE FROM THE BOMB-RUINS.

Bromley, Eng:  It was a great day at this Kentish
town when Princess Elizabeth laid the foundation stone
of the new Parish Church here.
The old church was destroyed by a bomb in 1941, but
the 500-years-old tower was undamaged.  The new church
is to be built onto this.
Cost of the new church will be between £70,000 and
£80,000 - part of which will be paid by the War Damage
compensation, and the rest will come from public appeals.
This was the first time that Bromley had received an
heir to the throne.
PHOTO SHOWS:   With a Guard of Honour of Boy
Scouts, Princess Elizabeth is greeted on her arrival
at the Bromley (Kent) Parish Church, where she laid
the foundation stone.
                October 13th. 1949.   PN-h.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672/3

THE HERRING HARVEST.

Hundreds of Scotch girls are engaged at Great Yarmouth on the herring
harvest. The girls gut the fish, repair the nets, and keep a
mountainous pile of barrels ready for packing the fish. The river Yare
is now packed with drifters and millions of herrings are being landed
almost every day. A new scheme of rationing the herrings to prevent a
glut is in operation at Yarmouth. Drifters are not allowed to
leave port at certain times and this frees the North Sea herring grounds.

activity: John Jamieson warping for a personal tweed on a loom of his own invention during the Highland Home Industries Exhibition at the Tea Centre in London.

te.text:
HIGHLAND INDUSTRIES COME TO LONDON, MJH/HT.

Highland Home Industries is this week holding a six day
exhibition and sale at the Tea Centre in Regent Street,
where beautiful hand made products from the Scottish
Glens and Western Isles are on view. To the Scottish
crofters in their lonely homes, the work of the H.H.I.
is of vital importance as it enables them to make a livelihood
in their own home districts, thus stopping the drift to
the towns which was in danger of depopulating the Highlands.
It also keeps alive the skilful crafts which would otherwise
die out.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: JOHN JAMIESON of Morar Invernesshire,
warping for a personal tweed he is to weave on the loom
of his own invention during the Highland Home Industries
Exhibition. John Jamieson who comes from the Isle of Unst
one of the most northerly of Scotland, appeared in "What My
Line" last night but did not beat the panel.
FOX PHOTOS NOVEMBER 15TH, 1954.

FOX PHOTOS
LTD.
69/71 FARRINGDON ROAD,
LONDON, E.C.1.

te.text:
MAN-MADE FOG USED TO BEAT INSECT PESTS.
21.5.47.
A demonstration was given at Thurton
Copse, near Andover, today, of the Todd
Insecticidal Fog Applicator, known as "Tifa".
Tifa, is a one-man controlled machine and is
designed to produce a fog of insecticide,
fungiside or hormone.  The substance to be
applied is mechanically atomised and introduced
into the atmosphere as a true fog in which the
chemical agent is uniformly distributed, and
provides an entirely new method of applying
insecticides to pests in buildings and open
spaces.
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS.  The Todd Insecticidal
Fog Applicator, using kerosene oil,
spraying a copse, during the demon-
stration today.  It can be mounted
on a Jeep, and is one-man operated.
RBN/H.keystone.

activity: 72-year-old silversmith Albert Middleton working at his bench in the jewellery quarter of Birmingham

te.text:
THE SILVERSMITH
YOU read maps to see the geography of Britain. You read
faces to see the character.
Here, at a silversmith's bench, is the face of the craftsman.
Deeply etched in the face of Albert Middleton, as surely as the
hallmark in his silver, are the qualities of infinite patience, quiet
pride in his skill — and unflappability.
Mr. Middleton is 72, But they retire late in this business. His skill,
gained from 58 years at the bench is too important to lose. So he
works on in the jewellery quarter of Birmingham, one of the ancient
homes of the industry, where there are at least 250 jewellery-making
firms.
Britain's jewellery trade is meeting fierce competition from the
Continent. But it is the designers who must face up to the challenge.
The craftsmanship, like that of Albert Middleton, remains untarnished.
Picture by DICK WILLIAMS.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
16 SEP 1963

activity: a new block of council flats in Croft, Leicestershire, which are criticized by villagers for looking like a prison

te.text:
WILLIAMS  SUN  17.7.66
"LOOKS LIKE A PRISON".
O.P.S.  Flats in Croft, Leics., which cost £30,000 are claimed to look
like a prison.

FLATS
THEY
CALL
THE PRISON
ANGRY VILLAGERS are to demand that a new block of
council flats should be pulled down. They claim the block
looks just like a prison.

"It's an absolute monstrosity," one villager said
last night. "If a private builder dared to build
such a thing the council would be the first to
object."
The £30,000 flats at
Croft, Leics, are being
built of concrete sections.
Work on them is almost
finished.
But the villagers want all
work on the "prison" to stop.
Their parish council have
asked Blaby Rural Council to
meet a village deputation as
soon as possible to hear
demands for the demolition
of the building.
EYESORE
Yesterday Mr. Don Wood,
who lives opposite the flats
in Broughton Road, Croft,
said: "If the council had set
out to create an eyesore
deliberately they could not
have done a better job."
Another Broughton Road
resident, Mr. Ian Woollard,
declared: "If we fail to get
satisfaction we shall go to
the Ministry of Housing and
Local Government."
His neighbour, Mr. Charles
Saxton, added: "Someone
has made an almighty mis-
take in putting up this mon-
strosity. It must come
down."
Mr. Thomas Heap, Clerk of
Blaby Rural Council, said:
"These are the first flats of
this type we have erected.
We didn't expect this
uproar."

activity: Eugene Gillespie, an engineer for the Irish Peat Board, with the world's largest plough, designed for digging drains in Irish bogs.

te.text:
IRISH NEWS AGENCY COPYRIGHT PHOTO
13/16 Fleet Street Dublin Phone 79821/5

NEWBRIDGE, Co. Kildare: It's the largest plough of its type in
the world. It will dig a drain 4 feet deep by 2½ feet wide, and
it has been designed and built at the Newbridge (Co. Kildare)
research station of the Irish Peat Board for use on Irish bogs.
Eugene Gillespie, 38-years-old engineer who conceived this
monster, comes from Gortnahork, Co. Donegal. He is modest about
his achievement. "It's just another plough", he says. Only
reluctantly he admits that when it goes to work, it will dig
the biggest drains in the fastest time yet. The monster took
two months to build - weighs over 1½ tons, has drum
wheels measuring 6 feet by 3 feet 6 ins. and will be drawn
by a tractor. It will be ready for testing in about a fortnight.
If produced commercially, it would cost about £750. When the
plough has been tested and approved, the design will be turned
over to a factory for production. Up to now, the largest
plough used by the Board can cut to a depth of only three feet.
IRISH NEWS AGENCY PHOTO SHOWS: Eugene Gillespie, Irish Peat
Board engineer, with the plough -- largest of its type in the
world -- which he designed for use on Irish bogs. INA

RCD. 14 APR 1952

HOUSING DEVELOPMENT & CONSTRUCTION LTD.
PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS
The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to
the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations and to the
specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B.
It only required three weeks of normal working with a very
small team of men to complete this pair of houses for
occupation. This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time
of any system of truly permanent housing for local authorities
yet developed.
Under this new system, a wide variety of external finishes
to the houses is possible, so avoiding the monotony to which
most industrialised systems and much traditionally built
housing is prone. Internally, room arrangements are extremely
flexible and can be rearranged very quickly and at negligible
cost, to suit individual needs and changes in size of family.

activity: The Rev. Bertram Peake preaches from the pulpit of Golborne Church to a congregation including former prisoners, with washing hanging in the gallery above.

te.text:
STRANDED EX-CONVICTS FIND A HOME IN A CHURCH
A NEW USE FOR EMPTY PEWS IN KENSINGTON

In the Royal Borough of Kensington there is a church where
every night stranded ex-prisoners and other unfortunate wrecks
of humanity find a place to sleep and call their temporary home.
In the gallery over the pews, and with a view of the altar and
the organ, they roll out their mattresses and get a peaceful
night's sleep, their washing strung out on a line from side to
side of this unusual place of worship. Their stomachs are well
filled with sausage and mash cooked by one of their number in
the church kitchen. No charge is ever made for all this, and
many of them are enabled by thus having an "address" to get
public assistance and then employment - so difficult for a
man with nowhere to go when he leaves his prison after paying
society's price, or for those other men who have fallen on
hard times and for who the Welfare State doesn't cater.
The Rev. Bertram Peake - known in the war as "The Tin Hat
Pastor" - who refused all honours for his work among the blitzed
Londoners, - has found this new use for his old church a
satisfactory continuation of his good, although to some minds,
unorthodox, work of caring for men's bodies as well as souls.
No man is refused at Golborne Church. No charge is made.
Men stay there on average six weeks. For many hope and faith
are renewed, and jobs found before they move on. But there are
always more who come to take their place in the gallery of
comfort in this Kensington Church.
KEYSTONE JP/13740

JP/13740-1 THE SERMON BENEATH THE WASHING

The Rev. Bertram Peake preaches from the pulpit of
Golborne Church, Kensington. Before him in the pews are his
"flock", many of them former prisoners. Above him,
not quite hidden, in the gallery, is their washing hanging out
to dry, and their beds. The pulpit was presented to the church
by the brother of a professed Atheist who made this last
bequest to the Rev. Peake when he was dying.

DAILY HERALD
15 JAN 1959

activity: General view of a Sunday market held in a cowshed on a farm in Buxted.

te.text:
BLANDFORD.SUN.28.11.65.
FARM USED AS MARKET.  Story Arnold.
O.P.S. Notices regarding the closure of the market.

IN these days of quick-dried, deep-frozen, pre-packed foods, the label "Farm-fresh" has an almost magical quality. Everything is certainly farm-fresh at this regular Sunday market — and nearly 500 people turned up yesterday to stock up on eggs, potatoes, butter and cream. Farmers from all over Sussex take their produce to the market which is held in the cowshed on Mrs. Sarah Lloyd-Jones's farm at Buxted, near Uckfield. They shout their wares, joke with the customers and give the whole place the air of a countrified Petticoat Lane. Their favourite spiel is that if you turn up early enough you'll find the eggs still warm from the hen, the milk still bubbling and the brussels still glistening with dew. They like to tell, too, of the man who makes a three-hour train journey from Hounslow, Middlesex, to shop for a whole streetful of people. He didn't show up yesterday. 
 By HARRY ARNOLD 
 Picture by LEN BLANDFORD 
 But people did come from 50 miles around, turning the thing into a jolly country fair. The farmers started it as a protest against the price review. They sell at average prices but make more profit with no middlemen or retailer to pay. But the market has proved too successful. And Uckfield Rural Council have issued a closing order. They have never liked the enterprise and chairman Stewart Mac-Kinney, a farmer himself, yesterday explained why. The council, he said, claim the market is unnecessary and is held on agricultural land. Parking facilities are inadequate and traffic congestion is caused in the village every Sunday. At the door of her cowshed, Mrs. Lloyd-Jones, chairman of the local committee of the National Farmers' Union, talked of an appeal against the closure order, backed by a petition from the customers. "No one," she said, "has the right to stop us giving this service. We do not sell at cut-prices." She added: "The reason we are popular is simply that everything is farm-fresh." And at the end of the day there was £600 in the tills to prove it.

activity: Princess Elizabeth holds the newly-christened baby Michael outside the church in Mersham

te.text:
PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RCB. 27 JUN 1950 
 TO 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 ART LIBRARY

200360 AND
PRINCESS IS BABY'S GODMOTHER

Mersham, Kent, Eng; Princess Elizabeth, who is
expecting her second baby this summer, attended a
christening ceremony in the tiny church here as a
godmother. The baby christened, five-weeks old
Michael John Ulick, is the second son of Lord and
Lady Brabourne.
For the Princess, it was her second visit to Mersham
since her wedding. Last summer she watched her husband
play for the local team in a cricket match.
The new baby's three-year-old brother, Norton Louis
Philip Knatchbull, has the Duke of Edinburgh as a god-
father.
PHOTO SHOWS: Princess Elizabeth holds the newly-
christened baby Michael outside the church in
Mersham. In the rear are the Earl and Countess Mountbatten,
and (extreme right) Lord Brabourne with his three-year-
old son Norton.
26th June, 1950 PN-b

PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672/3.

activity: igloo-shaped temporary houses made of reinforced paper corrugated fibre board

te.text:
Igloo-shaped home out of reinforced paper

P APER HOUSES are no longer just a flimsy idea. Prototypes, produced by the London firm of Tri-Wall Containers Ltd., have finished final tests and models should be on the market next year.
The temporary houses are one-storey, igloo-shaped units made from a very tough reinforced paper called corrugated fibre board.
They can be weatherproofed against most climatic conditions and will last for at least a year.
Building them can be very quick. A team of four men can put up a paper house in three hours—and demolish it in minutes.
Originally designed for emergency use in disaster areas, the houses are built by stapling together identical fibre board panels into hexagonal shapes.
Each panel supports another so that when they are all in place the houses stand firmly without any other help.
Larger buildings for use as schools and hospitals can be made by leaving out panels in a number of units and joining them all together into circular blocks.
Single living units have a door with adjoining glass window at the front and rear. They stand 10ft. high at the centre peak and have a 20ft. wide floor space. Plumbing and electricity can be installed normally.
Apart from disaster relief, the houses can also be used for workmen on isolated building sites. And in some cases they can even be cemented on the outside to become semi-permanent.
The price of a paper house has not yet been worked out, but Tri-Wall expect it to be in the region of £150.

activity: manufacturing the coronation carpet on large looms in a Glasgow mill

te.text:
MAKING THE CORONATION CARPET ON THE LARGEST
LOOMS IN SCOTLAND. 10.3.37.
The carpet that is to be laid in Westminster Abbey for
the Coronation ceremony is now being carefully made in a Glas-
gow mill. The carpet has several special features. It is one
of the biggest ever made, the pieces, of which there are many,
are 40ft. x 35ft. and the surface is getting special treatment
to make it as smooth as glass, this has been found necessary to
allow the flowing trains of the royal ladies and peeresses who
will walk on it, an easy passage, as any minute obstruction would
catch in the frail material they will wear. The carpet, owing
to its gigantic size, is being made on the largest looms in
Scotland, of messrs. TEMPLETON of Glasgow, who also made the
Coronation carpet for George V when he was crowned in 1912. The
Scots girls who are now working on the carpet, feel delighted
to be sharing in the work for this historic ceremony and are
taking extra special care at all stages of progress to produce
the finest example of carpet making.
O.P.S. Some idea of the size of the pieces can be gathered from
this row of girls working on the loom that is making the
carpet. HHS/B, KEYSTONE.

COPYRIGHT
KEYSTONE
VIEW COMPANY
PHONES -
CENTRAL
9634-5-6-7
12/13, WINE OFFICE CT.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, Feb 17th.

FIRST 8-STOREY LCC FLATS OPENED TODAY

Needwood House, Woodberry Down Estate, Stoke Newington -
the first eight-storey block of flats erected by the
LCC - are being opened today, Thursday. The block is
one of four now being erected; they have private sun
balconies adjoining the living rooms, electric fires in
living room and first bedroom, and the block is centrally
heated by a hot-water system fed from a sunken boiler
in the courtyard. Accommodation on the whole estate
will be provided for 1,765 families, or about 6,350
people in a variety of flats, maisonettes and two-storey
houses.

te.text:
AMERICANS VISIT TO RURAL CRAFTSMEN. 		DH/ME

A party of Americans made a tour of the Whiteway Colony
near Stroud, Glos., to see the work of members of the
Guild of Gloucestershire Craftsmen, who live in the
Colony. A good deal of the work of these hand craftsmen,
found its way to America before the war.

Photograph shows - Miss Mary Collins Powell, of the
American Red Cross and member of the U.S. Forces,
interested in the work of Mr S. Randolph who has been
making sandals for over 30 years. He took the business
from Edward Carpenter the socialist poet and writer. At
present Mr Randolph has enough orders for the next two
or three years. Miss Collins Powell is from Tarboro,
N. Carolina.
FOX SEPT. 10th 43.		300400-4.

activity: weaving baskets for airborne troops

te.text:
FIRST PUBLICATION EVENING PAPERS.
FRIDAY, DECEMBER 31st. 1943.

BASKET MAKERS PLAY THEIR PART IN
INVASION PREPARATIONS

Many of the air borne supplies
dropped to Allied airborne units
will be packed in hampers, for
the cushioning power of basket
construction makes it superior
to all other materials for
certain purposes. One London
firm of basket makers, Scott's
of St. Giles-in-the-Fields,
have been in the trade since
1661, and today their weavers
are working at top pressure to
fill "invasion" orders. Most
weavers are elderly, basket
making being a dying art before
the war, and with the raising
of Basket making to priority
status willow rods have been
brought across the Atlantic
from the Argentine.

PHOTO SHOWS:.. Mr. George Chappell,
aged 68, who has been weaving
baskets for 55 years, making one
of the hampers which will carry
supplies for airborne troops.
And. December 31st. 1943 PN

3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C.4.
PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3673

MALINDINE.          10.11.38.
Police reinforcements called to a baby show, at
Upton Park. E. this afternoon.
Two to three hundred babies were expected at
St. Stephen's Church Hall for the Show.  Some
15,000 turned up taking the authorities by
surprise. When some three or four hundred mothers
were told no more entries could be accepted
they refused to leave.  It was then extra
police were sent for to peruaade the mothers to
go.
O.P.S.
Crowd of mothers and babies outside the hall
despite the fact they were told they could not
enter.

activity: Mrs. SALTER and Miss HAIGH working in an Enfield furniture factory transitioning from aircraft manufacture to producing utility bedroom suites for the Board of Trade, with 'Mosquito' wings visible in the corner.

te.text:
V. 24050.
FROM BOMBERS TO BEDROOM SUITES ONCE MORE.
Four "Mosquito" aeroplane wings stand cradled in one
corner of an Enfield, Middlesex, furniture factory,
where men now mass-produce utility bedroom suites for
the Board of Trade. Poles apart in their symbolism,
they represent the switch-over from Peace to War - and
back again to Peace. They are reminders of what, less
than four years ago, was one of Britain's top secrets.
This factory hopes to produce 1,000 bedroom suites per
week in the near future to fill Britain's needs.
Picture shows; Mrs. SALTER and Miss HAIGH, who
worked all through thr war on aircraft manufacture -
now doing equally important work.
SUPPLIED  L. N. A.

D.H.    Spencer.    8.2.56.
Badges worn at Liverpool Clothing Factory.

At thefirm of John Peck & Co. Ltd, in Edge
Lane, Liverpool, (who make overalls, and
industrial clothing) the employees wear
badges, stripes and flashes, denoting
their qualifications. They can earn [crossed out text] 
extra money as they progress in their jobs,
the badges showing their efficiency.

a white coated trainee charge hand ("Lieut.")
who only four years ago was a trainee herself
shows the correct way to hem material to
three of the firms trainees, whose stripes
show their progress. They are left to right,
Sheila Bourke (L/cpl), Angela Landrum (Cpl)
and Kay Meskell (Sgt.) - all of Liverpool and
all 15 yrs of age.

activity: handling a geophone assembly on the deck of a vessel during a geophysical survey for oil off the British coast

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S DAILIES.....NOV.26th '56.

SEARCHING FOR OIL IN BRITISH WATERS.
                                      26.11.56.
The first water-borne geophysical survey to be carried
out by the British Petroleum Oil Company of the British
Coast took place recently, in the 1000 ton converted corvette
"SEISLIM", the first British-owned vessel to be specially equipped
for this work, off Swanage and Lulworth Cove. The purpose was
to investiaget the nature of the rocks beneath the sea bed
at 10,000 ft. B.P. has been carrying out a search for oil-
bearing rock formations in the British Isles for [strikeout] 21
years and this was its latest effort.
Charges were exploded four and half feet below the surface
of the water, along a previus plotted line. Vibrations
transmitted into the sea bed and reflected back from various
rock formations were picked up by detectors towed behind the
ship. They were then record electrically on a time chart
which is afterwards analysed by experts at The British
Petroleum Compnay's London Office.
                         Picture shows
Floating cable with geophones mounted on paravanes stored
on deck on completion of day's operations. E.K. LOVELOCK is
handling a geophone assembly.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
25 NOV 1956
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THEY SWEAT FOR BRITAIN

te.text:
USUALLY there never seems to be enough
wedding cake to go round. The trouble is that
so many guests want to take pieces home for
their family, who dutifully make ecstatic noises
in celebration of its quality. Mr. Ronald Mardell
seems to have solved this quantitative problem.
For his wedding on Saturday he has ordered a
cake standing 4ft. 6in. tall and weighing four
hundredweight. It will go to the reception in
Luton, Bedfordshire, by lorry. The cake, which
took five days to make, contains 450 eggs, 76lb.
of sultanas, 70lb. of currants, 36lb. of butter, two
bottles of brandy and two bottles of rum. It is
covered with 76lb. of marzipan and 60lb. of icing.

mentioned in the Com-

activity: view inside the main machinery cabin of a walking Dragline excavator at an ironstone quarry

te.text:
THE BIGGEST "WALKING DRAGLINE" IN THE WORLD
JS                                       31.10.51.
The world's largest "walking Dragline" - with a jib 282 feet long
and a bucket weighing 22 tons and holding nearly 27 tons of
spoil when full - is now working in the ironstone quarries of
Messrs Stewarts and Lloyds at CORBY. Constructed by Ransomes and
Rapiers, Ltd it has taken four years to build and walks under its
own power taking seven-foot steps. The dragline is now removing
the strata covering the ironstone bed down to a depth of 100 ft,
hoisting the loaded bucket (a deadweight of about 50 tons) to
the top of the quarry, and slewing round to deposit the spoil.
Although the giant machine weighs 1600 tons, and in its working
position is 5ft taller than Nelson's Column, it is controlled
entirely by one man.
     The picture shows a view inside the main machinery
cabin where the 14 motors provide a total of 3,150 h.p.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RECD. 1 NOV 1951
PLEASE RETURN

LN 415799   UP/B   LONDON BUREAU

"THE MAN WITHOUT A FURROWED BROW":

MARKTOBERNDORF, Germany: The man without a furrowed
brow... who doesn't have to strain every muscle in concentration
but relaxes in a deck-chair under a colourful beach-type
umbrella is this farmer who operates a remote control set of
the first German tractor that moves about and ploughs a field
by remote control.

The tractor is manufactured
by the German Fendt-Werke of Marktoberndorf as an answer to
the acute shortage of farm labourers. Should the tractor
ever get out of control, it will stop automatically upon
touching any obstacles that are higher than ground level.
The future plans call for a remote control centre that can
operate several tractors at a time with the help of television
cameras installed at their operating places.

15th June, 1961 - pn-on

te.text:
"WARRIORS GRAVEYARD "
MAKES "FOOD" FOR BRITAIN'S STEEL MILLS   DG/PRI

With plans for re-armament under consideration
the shipbreaking yards of Thomas Ward's at Inverkei
-thing, Scotland, are working at top speed to
cut up the scrapped veterans of two world wars.
Hissing acetylene torches are carving up such
famous ships as "Royal Sovereign", Revenge"
Rodney" and Nelson, and hundreds of tons of
valuable scrap are sent back to the hungry
mills.

PHOTO SHOWS: "Drawing her teeth". While an oxy-
-acetylene burner cuts into the upper guns of
REVENGE ( 29,150 tons approx) . Workmen with sledge
hammers breaker the lower 15 inch turret guns into
"cheeses" Seven months continuous destruction still
leaves the gallant ship with fighting top and
superstructure to come down
FOX PHOTOS Sept 4th 1950 432872

te.text:
TURNING GOLD INTO BOOKS.

In spite of thousands of years of scientific research
a machine has not yet been invented to beat gold, with
the delicate manipulation which is essential to success,
and so the job is still carried on by hand, in almost
the same way as it was carried on in the time of Queen
Cleopatra, varying only in the fact that a bronze hammer
was used by the ancients in place of the steel one used
today, and that machinery forms a small part of the
early stages..
O.P.S.    Gold beaters at work, for hours on end these
          men beat away with their hammers until the
          squares and ribbons of gold are in leaves, only
          four millionth of an inch in thickness.
               JS/F      Keystone.

TOMLIN.1983-5236/90184                       26.7.40.
MANY HUNDREDS OF THE TOUGHEST FIGHTERS IN EUROPE,
THE FRENCH FOREIGN LEGION, FORM PART OF THE ARMY
OF ALL FREE FRENCH MEN UNDER GENERAL DE GAULLE.
They are encamped in the South of England and number
in their ranks men from almost every country except
Germany.  Some of them have fought in every campaign
for the last 17 years.  A number of them after
fighting in Norway and returning to France escaped
to England to join the army of all free French men.
These Legionnaires were the first to enter Narvik
and to capture the town.
O.P.S. A line of French Legionnaires
SPECIAL NOTE.
(All the men in this photograph consented to
be photographed because they had no relations
in France that could be victimised.)

activity: four men manning the lever of a large cider press at a mill

te.text:
CIDER WHILE YOU WAIT      DG/MAE

For more than a quarter of a century  farmers from the
Broadway , Worcestershire, district, have brought their
cider fruit to Mr. J. INGLES cider mill, and they see their
fruit made into the refreshing liquor on the spot.
Mr. Ingles makes about 1,000 gallons daily at this
time of year, and he charges about 2d per gallon
for pressing.    An electric mill reduces the apples
and pears to pulp, and it is then dealt with in the
usual way with large hand-operated presses.

PHOTO SHOWS: "All hands to the Press". Four men man the
lever of the great cider press. The fruit pulp is
placed in matting which is folded over to form
layers. A fullpress yields 120 gallons.

FOR PRESS OCT 18th 1949  L13306

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: collecting the cocoons at Lullingstone silk farm

te.text:
QUEEN'S CORONATION ROBE MAY BE WOVEN
FROM LULLINGSTONE SILK
July 5th 1952 PAR 30210-1 (L-R)

QUEEN'S CORONATION ROBE MAY BE WOVEN
FROM LULLINGSTONE SILK

Silk for the Queen's Coronation robe
is likely to come from Zoe Lady Hart
Dyke's silkworm farm at Lullingstone
Castle, Eynsford, Kent, where this
picture has just been taken. Lady
Hart Dyke wrote to the Queen offering
spun silk from which the Coronation
robe could be woven. The Queen,
through a lady-in-waiting, has written
to Lady Hart Dyke to say that she
would be pleased if the silk for her
Coronation robe could be supplied by
Lullingstone silk farm. As yet, no
detailed arrangements have been made.
Lullingstone silk was used in the
Coronation robes of the Queen Mother
and two Princesses at the King's
Coronation and also in the present
Queen's wedding dress.
Lady Hart Dyke started breeding
silkworms at her Lullingstone Castle
home in 1934.
PICTURE SHOWS:- MRS. EDNA CLARK,
of Farningham, Kent, collecting the
cocoons at Lullingstone silk farm.
The cocoon, containing a mile-and-a-
half of silk, takes the worm three
days to spin.
July 5th 1952 PAR 30210-1 (L-R)
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF MONDAY, JULY 7th.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 8 - JUL 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THE BP EXPLORATION COMPANY TODAY STARTED TO DRILL
AN UNDERWATER WELL TWO AND A HALF MILES OFFSHORE FROM
LULWORTH COVE, DORSET THE OPERATION IS BEING
CARRIED OUT FROM A SPECIAL BARGE ON FOUR 130-FEET
TUBULAR LEGS IN THE SEA BED 60 FEET BELOW. THE BARGE,
A SMALLER VERSION OF THOSE USED BY THE COMPANY IN THE
PERSIAN GULF, CAN BE RAISED 30 FEET ABOVE THE WATER
LINE. IT IS DESIGNED TO STAY OUT IN ALL WEATHERS AND
HAS ACCOMMODATION FOR 25 MEN.
THIS [WEREXXXE] THE FIRST OFFSHORE OIL WELL TO BE
DRILLED IN THE COASTAL WATERS OF GREAT BRITAIN. OFF-
SHORE WELLS HAVE BEEN DRILLED IN COASTAL WATERS
ADJOINING THE PRINCIPAL OIL-PRODUCING ZONES IN THE
MIDDLE EAST, THE UNITED STATES, AND ELSEWHERE. BP
ITSELF HAS DRILLED A NUMBER OF WELLS OFF THE COASTS
OF THE ARABIAN PENINSULA AND TRINIDAD AND HAS
DISCOVERED OIL IN BOTH AREAS.
THE DECISION TO DRILL AT LULWORTH BANKS WAS
TAKEN AFTER SEVERAL YEARS INVESTIGATION OF THE AREA
INVOLVING SUBMARINE GEOLOGY AND MARINE GEOPHYSICAL
WORK HAD CONFIRMED THE [NKXSERNE] PRESENCE OF A
POTENTIAL OIL BEARING STRUCTURE. IF OIL IS FOUND
IN QUANTITIES THAT JUSTIFY PRODUCTION FURTHERS WELLS
MAY BE DRILLED.

MR. JOHN WIGMAN(LEFT), A DRILLER, OF MANSFIELD,

activity: An operator carrying a 53lb. petrol-driven rock drill descending from a helicopter at the South Bank helicopter site during a demonstration.

te.text:
DEMONSTRATION OF WORLD'S LIGHTEST
PETROL DRIVEN ROCK DRILL.          MJH/HA.

On the Thamesside helicopter site at the
South Bank this morning, the Cobra rock drill
was demonstrated. Weighing only 53lbs. this
motor rock drill is claimed to be the lightest
"self contained" machine in the world. It is
designed for use in remote places and recently a
party of engineers climbed Kebnekajse, highest
mountain in Sweden carrying two of these drills
"pack fashion" on their backs.  The purpose
of today's demonstration, which was held in
connection with the Public Works Exhibition, was
to show how easily the drills can be transported
to isolated sites, and also to show their
efficiency.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:   An operator carrying one of
the 53lb. petrol-driven rock drills seen
descending from a helicopter after landing
this morning at the South Bank site, during
the demonstration.  This clearly shows how
compact and transportable the drill is.

FARMERS BATTLE TO SAVE THEIR CROPS...
GRAIN DRYING AT PADDOCK WOOD.

Work was at progress this morning at
the Grain drying centre - at Paddock Wood, Kent - which
is operated under the auspices of the Ministry of 
Agriculture - drying the grain - which has been soaked
by the continuous rainfall of the past months...

facing great losses - owing to the bad weather.

activity: damping the hair of a newly made wig at Wig Creations, Ltd.

te.text:
REVIVING THE DYING ART OF WIG-MAKING

The free supply of wigs under the National Health
scheme has increased the demand for them and brought
to light the problem of lack of labour in this trade.
A craft which requires patience, skill and painstaking
application, it does not attract young people, who can
earn more elsewhere, and so most of the wig-makers are
elderly people. Wigs are made from women's hair, costing
as much as five pounds an ounce, and the hair is knotted
2 or 3 strands at a time onto a foundation of French
silk net. Infinite care is then required to achieve the
correct shape and the necessary shade to give the hair
the necessary semblance of authentic growth.

INP PHOTO SHOWS: Miss Eleanor Jackson, one of the
workers at Wig Creations, Ltd., London,
damps the hair of a newly made wig,
after which it will be set to the
required style and placed in a drying
cabinet.

MINE DETECTOR CHECK ON RUBBER FROM MALAYA: 
176856/7(LUD). METAL STRIPS FOUND IN BALES AT LONDON DOCKS. 

LONDON,ENG: A mine-detector being passed over bales of raw 
rubber on arrival at the London docks from Malaya, following 
the discovery of iron strips inside some of the rubber which 
had been disrupting the machinery that processes the rubber, 
and caused buyers from America to refuse taking it.

trace the metal strips inside the rubber, Mr Abbot Low Moffat, 
of New York City(Chief of the Trades Division of the E.C.A. 
Trade Mission to the United Kingdom) suggested the use of 
mine detectors in locating the metal strips - a suggestion that 
has been followed with excellent results.

te.text:
First pictures of the production of Britain's first super-
sonic aircraft, the details of which have been shrouded in
secrecy for several years, are released today by British
Aircraft Corporation.  The aircraft is the English Electric
Lightning twice the speed of sound all-weather fighter which is
in large-scale production at English Electric factories at
Preston, Accrington and Samlesbury, all in Lancashire.  The
Corporation says that the production of the aircraft has been
the "most extensive and advanced programme ever attempted
by the British aircraft industry".

July 12, 1961.

From: A.C. Brothers, Press Officer, British Aircraft
      Corporation Ltd., 100 Pall Mall, London S.W.1.
      Telephone: WHItehall 1020.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
13 SEP 1961
PLEASE RETURN
TO

te.text:
Esten  D.H.  3.4.44
EPSOM PREPARES FOR OPENING OF RACING SEASON
Racing opens at Windsor on Easter Monday and 
trainers hope that it will be the last wartime
season. Victor Smythe of Epsom has 48 horses in
training this year, 35 of them untried 2-year olds.
The increase is mainly due to a greater allocation
of feeding stuffs, but labour is still a problem.
Vic Smythe solves this by being assisted by part-
time local labour to assist in riding and gallops.
One of these is an Irish nurse from a local hospital
who rides the horses in gallops with as much nerve
as her professional colleagues.
-----------------------------------------
EPSOM PREPARES FOR OPENING OF RACING --
OPS 3. Vic Smythe on left watches his string of
2-year olds across the Downs.

te.text:
FIFTEEN-STOREY BUILDINGS PROPOSED TO REPLACE
SLUMS IN CENTRE OF LONDON.

Fifteen storey buildings are proposed to
replace some of the worst slums in the
St. Pancras area of London.
Models of these buildings, which would be
modern in every detail with special provision
for old people, are to be shown in the
exhibition at the Housing Centre,
Suffolk Street, Londoh.
Special permission would have to be obtained
to erect buildings of this height in London,
and special provision would be made to
erect the houses sufficiently far apart to
provide no light obstruction.
Among the plans also to be shown at the
Housing Centre are modern buildings of the
Prince of Wales Kennington estate..
PHOTO SHOWS: A model of fifteen storey flats
for slum clearance in St. Pancras designed
by four students of the Architectural
Association School. Mr. B.A. Le Mare, one
of the students, is standing with the model.
G January 5th 1936 PN.g.

activity: Mrs. Taylor and her two children, Godfrey Taylor and Molly, producing glass eyes at their family workshop in London

te.text:
A FAMILY OF GLASS-EYE MAKERS.

Glass-eye making is an art handed down from father to son
for the last 150 years in the family of Mrs.Taylor, of
New Oxford Street in London. The Duke of Wellington was
one of the first distinguished customers of the firm, and
they still keep two of his artificial eyes in a little
museum - he had his artificial eyes renewed every year.
To-day, the actual production lies in the hands of Mr.
Godfrey Taylor, a young man of 22, who can make a perfect
glass eye within 30 minutes. His mother and his 24-year-
old sister Molly run the business side of their undertaking,
but they, too, are trained to 'make eyes' and can well
replace Godfrey should he be prevented from working.

O.P.S. Mrs. Taylor, the mother, with her two children at
their work; they have to carry out some rush orders and
all the three of them are busy producing glass eyes.
F/Bl. Keystone/Dallison 3354

KEYSTONE PRESS
FEATURE SERVICE, Ltd.
6, WINE OFFICE COURT.
FLEET STREET. E.C. 4.

3 cols
5 1/2 wide
P.I.
take off R. Hand
Side .

TONY EYLES. SUN. 16.5.68.
FLATS DISASTER.
O.P.S. Two ladies stand by their possessions after retrieving them from
the flats.

We'll never go back, say families
Once they had a home . . now all they have left are possessions
AN EMERGENCY centre was set up to house families made homeless by the collapse.
People living nearby arrived with pramloads of clothes and blankets.
But last night nearly all families had been temporarily housed with friends and relations.
Mr. Frederick Davies, Newham's Housing Manager, said: "We have been overwhelmed by offers and we do not think we will need to use the emergency centre which has been set up at Canning Town library.
He said nearby boroughs had offered to begin today looking for temporary accommodation for any of the homeless who needed it.
Earlier, some of the shaken families were allowed to collect their belongings from parts of the block which were considered safe.
Mr. John White came out of the building clutching his cat Tim. He said: "It mattered a lot to me to get Timmy."
Many of the families who escaped the crash have said they will not live in the flats again.
Mother-of-three Mrs. Iris Morgan said: "I could never go back."
And Mr. Alan Smith said: "Next time it will have to be a house or maisonette - no matter how long it takes."
As the first news of the crash came in, Poplar Hospital opened a whole ward which had been closed because of lack of staff.
Doctors and nurses as well as blood donors phoned the hospital offering help.

activity: construction of the aluminium superstructure of the liner Oriana at the Vickers Armstrong shipyard in Barrow-in-Furness

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S DAILIES...19TH AUGUST, 1959. 
 NEW TECHNIQUES IN BRITISH SHIP CONSTRUCTION. 
 LE. 19TH AUGUST, 1959. 
 WORK IS NOW WELL ADVANCED ON THE LARGEST ALL-WELDED ALUMINIUM 
 SUPERSTRUCTURE YET BUILT INTO A BRITISH SHIP, THE 40,000TON 
 ORIENT LINER, "ORIANA", AT PRESENT UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN THE 
 VAST YARDS OF THE FAMOUS BUILDERS, VICKERS ARMSTRONG, BARROW- 
 IN-FURNESS, SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED THIS AUTUMN AND WHEN COM- 
 PLETED WILL TAKE UP SERVICE ON THE AUSTRALIA AND PACIFIC RUN IN 
 CONJUNCTION WITH THE P & O LINER "CANBERRA", ALSO OF 40,000TONS, 
 WHICH IS TO BE LAUNCHED A FEW MONTHS AFTER THE "ORIANA". 
 IT HAS BEEN CLAIMED THAT THERE IS MORE ALUMINIUM BEING USED IN 
 CONSTRUCTION OF THE ORIANA THAN WAS USED IN THE PRIDE OF AMERICA'S 
 SHIPPING WORLD, FLAG-SHIP OF THE UNITED STATES LINE, THE 
 53,000TONNER, "UNITED STATES". THE REASON FOR THIS IS THAT PRE- 
 VIOUSLY WHERE ALUMINIUM HAS BEEN USED TO ANY GREAT DEGREE, STEEL 
 STIFFENERS HAVE BEEN ESSENTIAL TO HELP WITH THE INTEGRAL RIGIDITY 
 REQUIRED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF A LARGE SHIP OF PRESENT-DAY STAN- 
 DARDS. 
 THE ALUMINIUM SUPERSTRUCTURE WEIGHING JUST OVER 1,000TONS, COM- 
 PRISES FIVE DECKS, TWO BRIDGE DECKS, AND ALL UPPER WORKS. THE 
 TOTAL AREA OF BULKHEAD AND DECK PLATING OF THIS MATERIAL IS ALMOST 
 350,000 SQ. FT. 
 ABOUT 90% OF THE SUPERSTRUCTURE XXXXXNXNEXXXNSZXXDXE HAS BEEN ASSEMBLED 
 IN A PREFABRICATED FORM IN SHOPS ENTIRELY INDEPENDENT OF THE MAIN 
 YARDS. 
 THE COST OF THIS GIANT NEW SHIP, THE LARGEST PASSNGER VESSEL TO 
 BE CONSTRUCTED IN THIS COUNTRY SINCE THE ALL-TIME RECORD BREAKER, 
 "QUEEN ELIZABETH", 83,673TONS, IS £12 1/2M. 
 A MOST INTERESTING FEATURE OF THIS BEATIFUL NEW SHIP IS THE BULBOUS 
 FOREFOOT, THIS, IT APPEARS, ENABLES THE SHIP TO TRAVEL AT A VERY 
 MUCH HIGHER SPEED WITHOUT THE ADDED EXPENSE OF EXTRA POWER. A 
 FEATURE WHICH WILL NO DOUBT BE INCORPORATED IN MANY FUTURE BRITISH 
 SHIPS. 
 THIS PICTURE, TAKEN RECENTLY IN THE YARDS OF VICKERS ARMSTRONG, 
 SHOWS 
 ------------------------------------------------------------- 
 A VIEW FROM THE STERN OF THE ORIANA SHOWING THE SHEET ALUMINIUM OF 
 THE SUPERSTRUCOURE AS IT BEGINS TO TAKE SHAPE ABOVE THE STEEL HULL, 
 NOTE THE DIMINUTIVE FIGURES OF THE WORKMEN IN COMPARISON TO THE SHIP.

PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 19 AUG 1959 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO 
 ART LIBRARY

activity: Alec Odd weighing a finished cricket bat in a small corrugated iron workshop in Sutton, Surrey.

te.text:
WHERE THE BATS OF THE GREAT TAKE SHAPE

In a small corrugated iron hut in West St., Sutton,
Surrey, where Montague Odd, who died last June, made
cricket bats for W.G. Grace, his two sons, Alec and
Philip carry on the family tradition of craftsmanship.
Most of the delicate job is done by hand, the only
machinery being a wood lathe and binder for the handles.
The clefts of willow which will one day sent the ball to
the boundary, come from Essex, Surrey and Norfolk, and
are hung to be 'cured' for some 4 to 6 months, during
which time they lose about two pounds in moisture. The
cane for the spring comes from Sarawak or Manila, and
the shaping to size balance and shape are done with the
help of experienced hand and eye.

PHOTO SHOWS: Alec Odd weighing a finished bat in the
little workshop in Sutton.

FOX PHOTOS   460994             25th Feb., 1952

activity: Operators at the Royal Mint examining finished coins on a special overlooking machine during the process of making more coins for circulation.

te.text:
BRITISH MINT WORKS OVERTIME -
169716.(LUD). TO PROVIDE MORE CHANGE FOR WORKERS.

LONDON, ENG: Because of a scarcity of change, workers at
the Royal Mint, here, are being increased from 800 to 1,000-
working day and night in twelve-hour shifts.
With over £127,000,000 worth of coins in circulation -
double the amount in 1939 - firms often find difficulty
in filling pay packets with the correct amount. The momentary
shortage is an apparant mystery - but hoarding is blamed
for some of it.
The Royal Mint, the Government office where British money
is coined, stands on Tower Hill, and was erected in the
year 1810. The nominal head is the Chancellor of the
Exchequer, but the actual chief is the deputy Master, a
civil servant who is appointed by the First Treasury Lord.
Besides all money in circulation in England, all medals
awarded by the Crown are made at the Royal Mint, and certain
Colonies are supplied with silver and bronze coins directly
from this department.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Operators at the Royal Mint examining
finished coins on a special overlooking machine, provided
with moving canvas belts, during the process of making
more coins for circulation.

activity: an explosion taking place, watched intently by a handful of men at the Safety in Mines Research Station

te.text:
SAFETY IN MINES RESEARCH STATION.         WS/C

In a little colony of low lying buildings on a bleak
hilltop at Harpurhill, Derbyshire, a handfull of men are
fighting continually against the causes of coalmine disasters
Coal dust, under certain conditions is as dangerous as high
explosive and these men are experimenting every day to find
an effective emthod of combating the menace.  A four foot
wide tube to represent a mine shaft is filled with coal dust
and purposely exploded, then the burnt out dust known as
(after damp) a very poisonous gas, is analysed.  More deaths
are caused by the gas than the actual explosion.

Photo shows-  The explosion taking place, watched intently
by the men.
FOX. MAY 4th. 36.

I N a depression at the foot of a slope on
the Derbyshire moors, a few miles from
Buxton, two great black pipes, resem-
bling huge water-mains, stretch out for
half a mile.  These are the
experimental galleries in which
coal dust explosions are created.
Pit props and timbers are placed
inside, and pulverised coal is
scattered along the road.
A cartridge is fired by elec-
tricity, and with a bang a cloud
of dust bursts out at the end of
the gallery, to explode into a
great flame, after which the
deadly brownish clouds of car-
bon monoxide come rolling out
of the tunnel, while the props
and timbers, after travelling for
half a mile through the gallery,
may be hurled a hundred yards
or so from the mouth.

TOPICAL PRESS AGENCY LTD.,
[illegible] STREET,
LONDON, E.C.4.
CENTRAL [illegible]

activity: the interior of a modern broiler house where chickens are being fed and watered in a warm ventilated atmosphere

te.text:
FARM OR FACTORY? BROILER BUSINESS SETS A PROBLEM

THE RAPIDLY EXPANDING BROILER BUSINESS
WHICH HAS BROUGHT MILLIONS OF CHICKENS TO THE
BRITISH HOUSEWIFE IS CAUSING A PROBLEM FOR THE
MINISTRY OF HOUSING - FOR AT THE MOMENT THEY DO
NOT NEED PLANNING PERMISSION.
FARMERS ALL OVER THE COUNTRY HAVE ERECTED
MODERN SINGLE STOREY BUILDINGS TO HOUSE THOUSANDS
OF CHICKENS - ALL WITH AUTOMATIC HEATING, VENTILATION,
WATERING AND FEEDING.
THERE IS ALSO THE PROBLEM OF RATING WHICH,
AT THE MOMENT, IS ALSO CAUSING A PROBLEM - BECAUSE
THE FARMER IS INSISTENT THAT IT IS A FARM - BUT
LOCAL AUTHORITIES ARE MORE INCLINED TO TAKE THE VIEW
THAT IT IS A FACTORY.
THE MINISTER IS NOW CONSULTING LOCAL
AUTHORITIES AND FARMING INTERESTS TO SEE IF ANY
ACTION IS NECESSARY.
HOWEVER, ONE LOCAL AUTHORITY HAS ALREADY
REFUSED TO DE-RATE HATCHERY PREMISES AND BROILER
HOUSES - AT HUNTINGDON. THEY PROVED THAT THE RUNNING
OF A BUILDING CONTAINING BIRDS WAS NOT SUFFICIENT
TO ESTABLISH A RIGHTFUL CLAIM (AS A FARMER FOR THE
LOWER RATING). IT APPEARS THAT THE PLANNING
AUTHORITIES ARE ALIVE TO THE UGLINESS OF SOME OF
THE BROILER HOUSES - SOME OF THEM 200 FEET LONG -
WHICH ARE BUILT ON LAND WHICH IN ITSELF IS NOT USED
FOR FARMING.
PICTURE SHOWS:

THE INTERIOR OF A MODERN BROILER HOUSE. THE BIRDS
ENTER IT AT TWO TO THREE WEEKS AND EMERGE FIVE OR
SIX WEEKS LATER FOR THE TABLE.
DURING THAT TIME THEY HAVE BEEN FED, WATERED,
AND HOUSED IN A WARM VENTILATED ATMOSPHERE BUT IN
VERY SUBDUED LIGHT.
82704 20/10/59 JOHN TOPHAM

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
21 OCT 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

PROPERTY OF

RCD. 5 - SEP 1950
PLEASE RETURN
TO

"WARRIORS GRAVEYARD"
MAKES FOOD FOR BRITAIN'S STEEL MILLS    DG/PRI

With plans for rearmament under consideration
the shipbreaking yard of THOMAS W WARD, Inverkeithing,
Scotland are working at top speed to cut up
the scrapped veterans of two world wars. Hissing
acetylene torches are carving up such famous ships
as Royal Sovereign, Revenge, Nelson and Rodney
(already scrapped). Hundreds of tons of valuable
steel have already been sent to the ever hungry
steel mills.

PHOTO SHOWS: A general view of the "graveyard
of giants", REVENGE, and ROYAL SOVEREIGN lie
side by side while the hulk of NELSON is on
left in the distance. A year's work has been
done on the R. Sovereign; seven months on
the Revenge.

FOX PHOTOS  Sept 4th 1950  432875

6, TUDOR ST.,

activity: Two boys who escaped a building collapse with their friends.

te.text:
DAILY
HERALD
14 JUL 1961
PLEASE RETURN TO
ART LIBRARY

Two of the boys who escaped . . seven-year-old John Frewer, left, and
Billy Cox, centre, with their friends.

A NINE-YEAR-OLD boy was killed and five other boys were injured last night when the roof of a derelict house caved in.

The boys were trapped under girders and piles of bricks and wood before rescuers managed to free them.

Mothers of the boys and men from a public house near the building, clawed at the debris with their bare hands.

Firemen with flame-cutting apparatus worked stripped to the waist.

The boy who died in the three-storey house in Anthony-street, Stepney, was Robbie Jitterbo.

Four of the injured boys were detained in London Hospital.

They are Robby Hatton, aged nine (face, head and neck injuries), and Michael Meah, aged 10 (leg and face injuries), both of Montefiore House, Cannon Street-road, Stepney; Tommy McLaughlin, aged 14 (head injuries), of Anthony-street, Stepney, and Nino Casser, 12, (back and leg injuries), of Cannon Street-road.

William McLaughlin, Tommy's 12-year-old brother, was treated in hospital, but went home later.

He crashed through their "den" in the building. They were playing on the roof 40ft. up trying to reach the branches of a pear tree.

One boy who escaped before the house caved in was Michael Shields, aged 13, of Montefiore House.

He said later: "I was swinging on a branch of the tree trying to pull it down when the roof collapsed.

"I was left hanging 15 feet up.

"I jumped down to see if I could get the other boys out. But I couldn't.

"So I ran to a telephone box and told the police to come very fast because some boys were trapped."

Mrs. Catherine McLaughlin, aged 52, mother of Thomas and William, said she heard a crash and screams and saw the building falling.

She added: "I sprang across the road. Through a cloud of dust I could see tons of wreckage piled up in front of me.

"I realised both my boys must be trapped."

Eleven-year-old David Meah saved the life of his 10-year-old brother, Mike.

David said: "I saw Mike's leg sticking out from a heap of bricks. I ran over and started to lift the bricks from his body."

DAILY HERALD
Copyright
Photograph.
By D. EATWELL
NUMBER........

activity: seventy builders working an extra unpaid half-hour on Bexley Council's housing site to support the government's housing drive

te.text:
“HALF HOUR FREE FOR THE
GOVERNMENT WE CHOSE”

SEVENTY builders on Bexley Council's housing site at Westwood-lane, Welling, Kent—already working nine hours a day—yesterday worked an extra half-hour, without pay.
They were carrying out the pledge they made on Wednesday, to help Mr. Aneurin Bevan's drive for 30,000 more homes by Christmas, and they will go on until the block of houses they are working on is finished.
Said one of them: “We reckon the Labour Government we elected will stand or fall on its housing policy, and we are going to do our level best to see that it stands.”
Because the union agreement only allows them to work one hour's paid overtime a day—which they are already doing—they decided to work the extra 30 minutes for nothing—clocking in 15 minutes early in the morning, and cutting the lunch hour by 15 minutes.
Mr. C. J. Pepper, the council's building superintendent, who came in an hour early yesterday, said:
“We hope to have the first house on the site ready for occupation in three weeks. It will go to the first family on our priority list, which now numbers well over 4,000 names.”

DUPLICATE SENT MANCHESTER
26 SEP 1946 PER MAT BOX

Men work an hour for nothing
to get houses done at Welling

te.text:
225756    QUI
M. P. CHECKS UP ON SCRAP METAL COMPLAINT
AFTER DOCKERS' PROTEST

Southampton: Mr Ralph Morley, Labour Member of
Parliament for Itchen, Southampton, inspects the
stacks of scrap metal which has been the subject of
protest by dockers. This scrap is due for shipment
from the Town Quay here.
An immediate inquiry into exports of armoured vehicles
is being urged by Mr Morley, to whom dockers have
protested that, while Britain's shortage of scrap is
acute, thousands of tons of steel are being shipped
in this form.
The M.P. has complained to the Ministry of Supply and
the Board of Trade and will raise questions in the House
of Commons to get these shipments banned.
Ex-Army equipment now awaiting shipment at Southampton,
say local dockyard experts, is worth thousands of pounds.
It could be melted to make first-class fighting equipment,
and much of it could be repaired.
21st January 1952    PN-b

te.text:
By PHILIP PHILLIPS
MILLIONS of viewers saw and heard the Duke of Edinburgh fluff a “cue”
during his International Geophysical Year broadcast from Lime Grove
last night. “Now we go over to Greenwich,” said the Duke, who was linking
up the £20,000 programme. But we didn’t. Instead, we got a picture of the
11,000ft. Jungfrau in Switzerland.
For a few seconds this pic-
ture filled the screen. Then
we were taken back to the
studio—and the Duke.
With an emphatic gesture of
annoyance, he said: “I’m afraid
I made a mistake there.”
He walked over to a 6ft.-high
globe and pointed to the Ant-
arctic. Pictures of snowy wastes
followed.
GOOD EVENING
Lights mark the world’s watchers

activity: washing machines in deserted storerooms at the Rolls Razor factory

te.text:
ROLLS RAZOR STORY
P.C. INTERIOR VIEW AT
FACTORY TO-DAY
CRICKLEWOOD H.Q.

DAILY HERALD
Copyright
Photograph
BY L. BLANDFORD
NUMBER...........

The showrooms . . there were still customers, but no sales
In the showroom window, notices still advertised a "continuous demonstration" of the firm's latest washing-machine.
Customers were still turning up. Still wanting to buy. Still convinced that nowhere else would they find such value.
One housewife travelled 20 miles to get a refrigerator. "It doesn't make any difference to me," she said. "I don't care what's happened. I want one."
She went home, however, without one. No one was selling. The showroom stayed closed.
"It's a shame," said one salesman. "We could sell lots. Customers are scrambling to get machines while they can."
But as the afternoon wore on the confidence of the men still waiting outside began to fade.
To vanish with the news that there was to be no fight. That this was the end.
The salesmen, despondent but even then half-disbelieving, held a meeting. And pulled out £1 notes to pay for a solicitor to look after their rights.
They claimed the firm owes them about £150 each in wages and retention money—a sum held in security against the stock they carry.
But not all could so easily give up hope. Salesman Bill Taylor, of Luton, stayed optimistic to the end.
He paid £20 in cash for a friend's £40 Rolls Razor cheque. Because, he said, "I know I'm still on a winner."

Blandford          DH          20.7.64.
Rolls Razor.
OPS...Shows washing machines in deserted storerooms.

activity: rustproofing technique for Morris cars at a special plant in Cowley

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS  18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.
Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 1 1/2 hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced 1/4-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

DAILY HERALD
ART LIBRARY
RETURNED UNDAMAGED

te.text:
KENT GIRL TO WEAVE MATERIAL FOR PRINCESS ANNE'S COAT.     MJH/RS.

Miss Mary Keer, aged 24, a weaving instructress at the Cathedral
Weaving Centre, Canterbury, is to weave the clothe for a coat
for Princess Anne from ten pounds of fleece which has been shorn
from a pet lamb, called Linda at the Children's Aid Society's
Andrew Duncan Home, which was opened by the Queen when she was
Princess Elizabeth. Miss Keer will spin the raw wool into yarn
on a spinning-wheel and then weave it into material which will
eventually make up the little coat. The Queen has asked that the
coat should be white.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Miss Mary Keer, aged 24 of Canterbury at work
on the Douglas Andrew "Kentish" loom, on which she will weave the
material for Princess Anne's coat. She is wearing a green cheviot
tweed costume, the material for which she also wove on this same
loom.

185964    DAW

MONEY AT HIS FINGER-TIPS.... NEW MINTING OF GOLD
SOVEREIGNS - BUT NOT FOR ISSUE.

London, Eng:- To preserve the knowledge of gold coining,
which has been handed down from craftsmen to craftsmen,
a small coinage of 100,000 sovereigns has been struck
at the Royal Mint here. They will not be for issue.
They were struck from the dies used for the 1925 issue.
(This 1925 issue was struck to replace light-weight coins
in the stock of the Bank of England. The general issue
of gold coinage was suspended in 1917). - Therefore the
issue which has just been struck bears the head of King
George V.
Further small mintings will take place in the future, but
again, only for the purpose of preserving the gold coining
craft.
PHOTO SHOWS:- After the process of 'striking' has
been completed, these sovereigns are poured into a bag to
be stored in the vaults.

activity: beer being poured down drains at Ansell's Brewery in Birmingham following a production strike

te.text:
HOLD UP COAT AGAINST LT BACKGROUND PLEASE -
& PIPE WITH BEER POURING FROM IT.

FIVE MILLION PINTS OF
WALLOP THROWN AWAY
A SAD sight for beer-
drinkers. That stuff
gurgling down the drain is
their favourite drink.
Exactly 250,000 pints of
it were poured away at
Ansell's Brewery in Birm-
ingham yesterday.
But worse is yet to come.
Another five million pints
will go down the brewery's
drains within the next few
days.
Which means that
wallop worth £370,000 is
being wasted.
Why? A spokesman for
the firm said: "Wastage
on this scale obviously
grieves our customers as
deeply as it does us."
But he explained that
the beer has been spoiled
because 1,300 production
and transport workers at
the brewery went on strike
claiming a cellarman shop
steward had been victim-
ised.
The spokesman added:
"We have had to write it
off because it would have
fallen below our high
standard."
Fresh ale should be
going out soon, because the
strikers decided at a mass
meeting last night that
they will return to work on
Monday.

activity: portrait of Fred Steel, a first furnace hand, in the light of his own fires at a steel works in Sheffield.

te.text:
Substitute
picture for
opening spread
of steel town

T
HE long, deep shop in the works, vast and dim,
where steel is made, where rows of furnaces
pour out their streams of running metal—this
is the heart of Sheffield, town of steel.
Before one of the furnaces stands a man whose name
is Steel. Fred Steel, first furnace hand, whose job is
one of the fiercest, most gruelling in the world. On the
left is his portrait taken in the light of his own fires.
He and his workmate had advanced before the opened
mouth of the furnace and with their twenty-foot irons
had just stilled the boiling steel. At furnace heart the
temperature reaches 1,670 degrees centigrade.
Fred Steel steps back, pushes his blue glasses from
eyes glazed with the heat; his open mouth sucks in
the cooler air, sweat covers his face, mats his hair.

activity: Mrs Florence Munro bringing a cup of tea to her husband P.J. Munro and H. Woodbridge as they build a 24-foot yacht in their back garden in Fulham.

te.text:
BACK-YARD BOAT-BUILDERS PLAN TO SAIL TO           D/HA
AUSTRALIA

Neighbours of Mr and Mrs P.J. Munro of Oxberry Avenue,
Fulham, can watch ship-building in progress  by looking
out of their back windows.  Mr. Munro, production
manager of cosmetics with a West End hairdresser, is
at present building a 24 ft. yacht in the back garden,
assisted by Mr. H. Woodbridge, and he and his wife hope
to sail to Australia.  Their only experience of sailing
so far has been on the Norfolk Broads, and Mr Munro has
been building his £500 boat from library books.  When
finished, the craft will be lifted into the lane at the
back, and launched at Putney, it is hoped this summer.

PHOTO SHOWS:  Mrs Florence Munro brings a cup of tea
for her husband, busy on his yacht-building in the back
garden. At left is Mr. H. Woodbridge, a building worker,
who is assisting him.

FOX PHOTOS    459352              16th Jan., 1952

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC. 17 JAN 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO

activity: wood turner Bill Evans teaching apprentice Gwyndaf Breese how to make wooden spoons at the Welsh Folk Museum

te.text:
GREAVES.   D.H.   26/3/54.
RURAL INDUSTRIES IN WALES.
At the Welsh Folk Museum at St.Fagans, near
Cardiff, many of the old crafts are kept
alive today, and by means of an apprenticeship
system it is hoped to preserve them forever.
Bill Evans who comes from Pembrokeshire has
been a wood turner since he left school 35
years ago. He carries on the old craft at
the museum, [struck through] making wooden bows, spoons etc,
by hand, using only the most simple tools.
OPS. He is seen here with apprentice Gwyndaf
Breese age 18 of Merionethshire. He is showing
Gwyndaf how to make wooden spoons.

FOR 35 years Bill Evans has
been a wood turner, first in
his native Pembrokeshire and
now at the Welsh Folk Museum,
St. Fagan's, near Cardiff.
Here he is, teaching 18-year-old apprentice Gwyndaf Breese,
of Merioneth, to make a wooden
spoon. He uses the simplest
tools, but each of his completed
bowls, spoons and other articles
is a work of art.

ART LIBRARY
PLEASE RETURN
TO
3 APR 1954

a drink. ALLAN comes from SEVENOAKS, Kent.

activity: overcrowding and slums at No. 39 Palmerston-road, Sparkbrook, Birmingham, specifically showing Kathleen nursing child Wiltree

te.text:
IT used to be such a nice, modestly pleasant road, built in the
days when the more prosperous clerks and artisans were moving
out from the city centre.
Its bow windows were the outward and visible sign that its
occupants had
socially arrived.

No-one doubts what is
Britain's most pressing social
problem. It is housing.
Today the landlords meet in Harro-
gate. They will air their grievances at
the annual meeting of the Federation
of Property Owners. ("The oldest
and largest national organisation
pledged to defend private ownership
and private enterprise" as their letter-
heading proclaims.)
Their grievances will be very much
as before—there's not enough money
coming from the tenants; there's too
much Government interference.
Not all tenants will agree. In all our
big towns thousands are being forced
by housing shortage into hideous over-
crowding at high rents.
As fast as old slums are demolished
new ones are created.
No. 39, Palmerston-road, Spark-
brook, Birmingham, is typical. It pin-
points a problem repeated in the
inner suburbs of every big city where
industry demands more workers.

By SIDNEY WILLIAMS, reporting from Birmingham

Now its older resi-
dents are thinking it's
about time they moved
from Palmerston-road.
They see that what's
happened all over
inner Birmingham has
started to happen here
—the same thing that
happened in Bays-
water, Paddington,
Notting Hill, Battersea
in London, and Moss
Side in Manchester.
People who can't get
a house or a flat to
themselves are crowd-
ing in to make what
they call a home in
the one room.
The authorities call
it "multiple occupa-
tion." They issue regu-
lations against it.
But they can do
little to enforce them.

From the Public Relations Division of:

WOOD & WEBSTER LTD., ACME CHAMBERS, BRADFORD ST., WALSALL.

Telephone: Walsall 21618 (3 lines)
Written by ............................
Publication Date ......................

HOUSING DEVELOPMENT & CONSTRUCTION LTD.

PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS

The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to
the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations, and to the
specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B.
It only required three weeks of normal working with a very
small team of men to complete this pair of houses for occupation.
This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time of any system
of truly permanent housing for local authorities yet developed.

   The 16 ft. x 12 ft. living room of the centrally heated
H.D.C. house is separated from the dining and kitchen
area by a glazed screen - just one of several alternatives.
All walls and ceiling have an unusually high degree of heat
insulation.

HARVESTING GOLDEN STANDARD MAIZE - SOME 50,000 COBS OF 
 GOLDEN STANDARD MAIZE BEING HARVESTED NEAR GUILDFORD.
 These are equal to those grown abroad and are the result
 of twelve years research of Mr. A. H. Kortland, a Dutch
 botanist and Poultry Farmer who escaped to this country
 from Holland after the Nazi occupation of the Low Countries.
 At this stage of growth this maize will stand up to eight
 degrees of frost without any ill effects. Many applications
 for seeds have been received from abroad including South Africa.
 This is the first time that this maize (which is essential
 for first class poultry) has been grown successfully in
 this country.

activity: Mr Stapley (left) taking delivery of a prize-winning silver rose-bowl after it had been Hall-marked.

te.text:
HALL MARK OF EXCELLENCE.      EH/HT

The silver rose-bowl, designed and made by Mr J. E. 
Stapley, of Whitstable, Kent, won the first prize
in the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths' competition
for a £500 piece of plate to commemorate the Festival
of Britain. Mr Stapley, who is a student at the Royal
College of Art, London, called to collect his prize-
winning piece after it had been tested by assayers at
Goldsmiths' Hall, and received the "Hall-mark" which
guarantees that the silver itself is up to the 
standard of fineness required by law.

Photograph shows :- Mr Stapley (left) taking delivery
of the rose-bowl after it had been Hall-marked. The
prizewinning rosebowl is to be shown at the exhibition
of British silverwork by modern craftsmen, which opens
at Goldsmiths' Hall on July 2nd.
FOX PHOTOS JUNE 18th 51.      449111.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 1 9 JUN 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: 70-year-old blacksmith Nathaniel Barber working at his forge at Milford Mill, near Salisbury.

te.text:
ESTEN   D.H.   1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years.  Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet.  He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1  70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
        at Milford Mill.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, June 25th,

PROGRESS ON BRITAIN'S AERIAL GIANT
25.6.47.
At the Bristol Aeroplane Works at FILTON, progress is being
made on the huge 125-ton "Brabazon I" landplane - the largest
ever to be built in Britain - which when completed will carry
100 people direct from London to New York. A special runway,
for which a complete village had to be demolished and which
will cost £2,000,000, and an assembly hall, are being con-
structed to get this giant into the air. She will have a wing-
span of 230ft (30ft longer than between the main structures
of Tower Bridge), and will be powered by eight Centaurus gas-
turbines of 2500 h.p. each. The picture shows

A view of the spacious interior of the "Brabazon" looking
toward the tail.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED
