te.text:
ROPER                                  16.5.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type. The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
Someofthe
Above is one of the machines used in the
Coplax process. Its object is to produce
the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.
OPS.

te.text:
"SQUATTERS" TAKE OVER AT REGENT'S PARK
---------------------------------------
22-8-46

"SQUATTERS" have moved into an Anti-Aircraft gun
site at Primrose Hill, near Regent's Park, London.
These huts were originally intended for Polish
soldiers and their wives, but the inevitable
squatters have now taken over. They are homeless people
who take the possession of empty army huts, gun sites
etc. without waiting for any official decision about
the future of the disused military camps. The movement
has spread recently all over Britain, and a deputation
of squatters went to Whitehall to ask the Government to
clarify their legal position.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:        Mr. and Mrs. C. CLARKE and
                           family, and Mr. and Mrs. J.
                           ROCHE, who were living in a
condemned house at Chalk Farm, now have neighbouring huts,
but for the present they are feeding communally until they
are really settled in.
PICTURE BY F. MOTT.

te.text:
JAGUAR LEADS THE WORLD WITH THE NEW E-TYPE: PRODUCTION STEPPED
UP BY 50%
Presenting the new E-type Jaguar - the car that's put
Britain ahead on the road, rocketed her dollar earning exports,
and is fast becoming the latest status symbol for up-and-comers
with an eye for a jazzy means of transport.
The brain behind the E-type is Mr. William Heynes, chief
engineer who joined Jaguar boss Sir William Lyons' Coventry
team in 1935. His new design is revolutionary - built up largely
from the racing Jag - but Mr. Heynes has, with some conservatism
and some criticism, retained the old Jaguar gear box.
A rush of orders was expected, but Sir William didn't
bargain for the need to step up production by 50%. Down in the
Coventry works extra night shifts are being put on to cope with
demand.
And even though buyers in this country will probably
have to wait about a year for a new model, orders still pour in
from discerning motorists for this super sports car that looks
good, moves fast - top speed is 150mph - and only costs just
over £2000.

activity: A view of a 12,000 ton forging press for aluminium alloy with a 550 h.p. treble-ram pump in the foreground.

te.text:
XML)   INAUGURATION OF EUROPE'S LARGEST FORGING
        PRESS FOR ALUMINIUM ALLOY

Europe's newest and largest forging press for aluminium
alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High	Duty Alloys, Ltd., by
the Chairman, Sir Frank Spriggs.  Known as "Goliath,"
this 12,000-ton press, the first of its type in Great
Britain, has been designed to give working pressures of
4,000, 8,000 and 12,000 tons.  The press itself weighs
800 tons and has an overall height of 56ft. 4in.  Of
this, 42ft 9in. is above ground level and the remainder
with the hydraulic system for operating the movable
table, is concealed below ground level.  It cost more
then £500,000.

Photo shows:--   A view of the 12,000 ton press with
one of the 550 h.p. treble-ram pumps in the foreground.

activity: A wine and apple tasting event organized by the Food and Wine Society and the Farm Produce Council.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
SUN
27 SEP 1967
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THE FOOD and Wine
Society, together with
the Farm Produce
Council, organised a
taste-in yesterday. Wine
and apples.
There were seven wines
and nine varieties of
apples. Combinations of
each amounted to 63
separate tastings. No one,
however, appeared to take
the risk.
There was more than an
outside chance of getting
stomach ache and failing a
breathalyser test, all at
the same time.
Piled up
The apples were brought
up from Tunbridge Wells
by Mr. Ben Tompsett,
chairman of the National
Farmers' Union Kent Fruit
Committee, and piled on
dishes next to chateau-
bottled Sauternes.
There were Laxtons and
Cox's and Lord Lam-
bourns, Russets and Alling-
ton Pippins.
Among the wines to be
tried with them were a
1940 Chateau Latour
Blanc, 1939 Chateau de
Rayne and a 1949 Chateau
Rabaud.
Not all of them mixed.
Several members of the
society suffered acute
withdrawal symptoms
after the third or fourth
slice of apple.
Others, however, were
more enthusiastic. The
idea, said Mr. Claude
Morny, secretary of the
Wine and Food Society,
was to remind members of
the different varieties, and
the subtleties of taste, of
English apples.
"But I'm not suggesting
that anyone should choose
a wine merely to suit a
particular desert apple," he
added.
Afterwards Mr. Tompsett
enthused: "I have been
staggered by the know-
ledge about apples which
has been displayed here to-
night. Unfortunately, I
had little chance to taste
the wine."

activity: Ronald and Pauline Potter look out of their bedroom window.

te.text:
Family in cellar get
a house
at last
By Betty Crisp
I WENT underground at Torquay yesterday to the two rooms and a cupboard where a family of six has lived for five years "under the pavements."
The Torquay cave dwellers were happy.
They had just heard that they would get the first council house available, instead of waiting till November as the Housing ommitCtee proposed.
Mother-Mrs. Doris Potter, aged 40-telephoned eldest daughter, Jean, 20-year-old shop assistant, with the good news.
Then she went off to tell father-Mr. Tim Potter, aged 47-a chef at a holiday camp.
Pauline, 11, and Ron, nine, jumped with joy when they returned from school and heard they would soon have a proper place to keep their two pet hamsters. And Anne, 14, at the technical college, could hardly believe that she and Jean would soon have their own bedroom.
I saw the bedroom they have shared with their parents and the younger children at Wellesley-road, for five years.
Three beds
The 14ft. by 11ft. room was crammed with a single and two double beds, a wardrobe and two chests of drawers.
But the furniture could only be seen when the light was on, for this is the room Mr. Gibbings said only got light from "a grating in the pavement."
There is a wall up to street level a few inches in front of the only window with iron bars on top.
The rain splashes in, for both window and the door into the sitting-room have to be kept open in all weathers so that the Potters can breathe.
The Council was told: "It is hardly fitting that the Queen of the English Riviera (Torquay's advertising slogan) should house a family of four children in what you can practically describe as cellars."
No window
The Potters' sitting-room, 14ft. by 12ft., has a normal window opening on to the sloping ground at the back of the house. Their third "room" is a cupboard under the basement stairs, once the coal hole, where Tim Potter has fitted a gas cooker and a sink.
There is no window, or ventilation, and not enough spare space to swing a mouse.
"I can hardly believe we are going to get a council house at last," said Jean, a pretty auburn-haired girl.
"Mum and Dad were on the Torquay list years ago. Then they had to go to Birmingham to work and when they came back in May, 1950, they were told they must go on the bottom of the list again and wait five years.
"It has been so awful having no privacy, especially as we children grow older. Fancy Anne and myself with our own bedroom. A real one with a window that lets in sun and air."
DAILY HERALD July 7 1955 3
Ronald and Pauline Potter look out of their bedroom window.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

ERECTING KENT'S FIRST ALUMINIUM SCHOOL
Ods 12.4.49.
The first of the five schools to be built by the Kent County Council
in aluminium prefabricated sections, is now well under way. The
school will be known as the Grays Farm County Primary School, and
is at St. Paul's Cray. The walls and roofs are of aluminium alloy
in prefabricated sections supplied by the Bristol Aeroplane (housing)
Company, and they are delivered to the site ready for erection. Thus
much time and labour, apart from materials, are saved. The block
illustrated in these pictures will house five classrooms and one
general purpose room. There will be another block housing two
classrooms and a general purpose room, an administrative wing,
assembly hall, canteen kitchen, dining hall, etc., and the whole
school will accommodate 360 children. The only brickwork will be
the external gable end walls and the boiler house, the foundations
of which can be seen in some of the pictures, which were taken
during a visit to the site today.

te.text:
CAMP PREPARED FOR ITALIAN WIVES BUT IT WAS
SEIZED BY BRITISH SQUATTERS.. 12-8-46

Thirty-six ex-Service men's families
have seized Vache Camp, Chalfont St. Giles. The
Camp was built for Americans at a cost of
£500,000, and was being prepared for the Italian
wives of [strikethrough]Italian[/strikethrough] Polish servicemen, but the British
Squatters settled in instead.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- The local butcher takes
orders this morning from Mrs. P. Gray and Mrs
O. Thompson, at the camp this morning.
ML/JSS KEYSTONE
2

First tradesman to visit the ex-Servicemen's families now
settled in at Vache Camp, Chalfont St. Giles, was the butcher.
He took orders for the weekly joint from Mrs. P. Gray and
Mrs. O. Thompson.

KEYSTONE
PRESS AGENCY LTD.

activity: Vera Green, the champion shrimp peeler of Scotland, demonstrating shrimp peeling at the Hotel and Catering Exhibition at Olympia, London.

te.text:
WHAT'S her line? Those
nimble fingers hold the
clue. She is the Champion
Shrimp Peeler of Scotland.
Her output: 2,500 shrimps an
hour. Her name: Vera Green,
from Annan, Dumfries. Vera
showed how it's done yesterday
at the Hotel and Catering Ex-
hibition in London.

20.1.54.
CATERING EXHIBITION OPENS.
A CHAMPION SHRIMP PEELER.

The Hotel and Catering Exhibition opened
this morning at Olympia. Vera Green, 20, who
is Scotland's No. 1 shrimp girl, was demonstrating
her skill of shrimp peeling on the stand of W. Young
and Son. In her little home town of Annan
on the Solway Firth she is this year's champion
shrimp peeler. Competing against 40 finalists in
an annual contest at the local packing station where
she works, she won a silver cup by peeling 13 pints,
or 2,500 shrimps, in an hour.
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- MISS VERA GREEN, seen
piling up shrimps ready to start picking,
at Olympia today.
H Keystone. BIR/616225

KEYSTONE

activity: the pineapple plant with the careful hand of MR. WILSON in the background.

te.text:
COPYRIGHT PHOTOGRAPH
JOHN TOPHAM LTD.,
16, HATHERLEY ROAD,

SCOTTISH BANANAS ! - AND A PINEAPPLE !

BELIEVE IT OR NOT BUT BANANAS AND A PINEAPPLE ARE
BEING GROWN IN SCOTLAND - NEAR INVERNESS !
THE MAN RESPONSIBLE IS 59 YEARS OLD DAVID WILSON,
HEAD OF THE HORTICULTURAL DEPARTMENT ON THE DOCHFOUR
ESTATES NEAR INVERNESS - AND HE HAS A BANANA TREE WITH
JUST OVER 200 BANANAS IN FRUIT. IN DECEMBER LAST YEAR
HE HARVESTED A PINEAPPLE - SINCE WHEN HE HAS SUCCESSFULLY
REPLANTED THE HEAD FOR ANOTHER FRUITING PERIOD.
MR. WILSON, WHO COMMENCED HIS CAREER IN THE CLYDE
VALLEY AT THE AGE OF 14 LOOKING AFTER TOMATO PLANTS, HAS
BEEN NURSING HIS BANANA TREE SINCE 19TH JANUARY, 1965,
WHEN HE PLANTED IT IN ONE OF HIS GREENHOUSES. HE HAS
KEPT IT AT A HEAT OF NEVER LESS THAN 60 DEGREES F. AT
NIGHT AND ALMOST 80 DEGREES DURING THE DAY - WITH A
HIGH HUMIDITY. THE PINEAPPLE, WHICH HE HARVESTED ON
23RD DECEMBER LAST TOOK HIM THREE YEARS TO GROW.
HE EXPECT TH BANANAS TO BE FULLY RIPE BY THE END
OF JUNE - AND THE PINEAPPLE - ABOUT 1968.

PICTURE SHOWS:
THE PINEAPPLE PLANT - WITH THE CAREFUL HAND OF
MR. WILSON IN THE BACKGROUND.
117275   10/5/67   JOHN TOPHAM

activity: Workmen preparing blocks for the removal of a port propeller from the ship Queen Elizabeth during its annual spring clean in King George V Graving Dock.

te.text:
THE "QUEEN" GETS A SPRING CLEAN
Q. ELIZABETH IN DOCK              DG/HT

Biggest spring clean of the year has begun on the
QUEEN ELIZABETH (83,600 tons) nof off the Atlantic
and high and dry in the King George V Graving
Dock at Southampton. Every day she stays in dock,
some 1500 men are busy inside and out on the giant
Cunarder. Their jobs include : the removal and
refitting of the giant screws; scraping and
examining every one of the thousands of links in
the cables; scraping and painting the outer bottom
and sweeping six miles of carpets.

PHOTO SHOWS:- One of the port propellors suspended
after removal from the shaft. Workmen below it
are preparing the blocks for removal.
FOX PHOTOS Jan 17 1950 418762

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 1 8 JAN 1950

te.text: F192 3D Home + HOUSING. PRE WAR / Slums MISC.

A FORGOTTEN HAMLET IN THE MIDDLE OF LONDON.
TO BE DEMOLISHED.                                   21.3.35.

        Not far from the noise of the East India Dock-road is
a little piece of forgotten London; a place where trams and
buses have never been, and where motor-cars are a rarity. The
Bow Creek, it is called. It is a hamlet at the mouth of the
River Lea, with just a few hundred inhabitants. Now the L.C.C.
want to demolish it, as it is described as being one of the worst
slums in London. The houses are 120 years old.
O.P.S.    A view of the houses in Bow Creek which are
          to be demolished.        JM/S  Keystone.

activity: A Policeman on duty outside the deserted Austin works at Longbridge, Birmingham, looking up at a 'fuel thermometer' notice

te.text:
FUEL SHORTAGE CAUSES AUSTIN SHUT-DOWN : THOUSANDS OUT.

All production employees of the Austin Motor Company's works -
14,800 in all - are affected by a shut-down of the factories caused
by the coal shortage.  Stocks of fuel are said to be so low that
it will be impossible to start work again unless the present
allocation is revised and delivery increased, and the works may be
closed for several weeks.
With coal distribution crippled by blizzards, hundreds of industrial
plants throughout Britain have had to close down temporarily, and many
thousands of workers have been thrown out of work.
PHOTO SHOWS:- A Policeman on duty outside the deserted Austin works
at Longbridge, Birmingham, looking up at a "fuel thermometer" notice
which shows just how much coal they have in hand.  The indicator
now reads "Heating Reserve", which is just enough to keep the factory
from freezing-up - but allows none to work with.
CHI.                9th February, 1947.             PN-s.

COPYRIGHT
-PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON. E.C.4.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, Jan 21st.
"QUEEN ELIZABETH" OF THE AIR TAKE SHAPE
21.1.47.
In the early summer it is hoped that the Bristol "Brabazon" pro-
totype of Britain's largest airplane, will make her first flight.
Work on the giant aircraft began just over a year ago, and her
construction will have involved an outlay of £4,000,000, the
destruction of a village and a golf course, and the building of
a special runway costing £2,000,000.
She will be 177ft long with a wing span of 230ft (30ft longer than
the distance between the main structures of Tower Bridge), and
weigh 130 tons, and eight Centaurus gas-turbines of 2500 hp each
will power her. "Brabazon's" later models will carry 100 passengers
in comfort at 250 mph on Britain's Atlantic services.
In this picture what looks like the framework of a prefabricated
house is an outer wing section of the "Brabazon" in which engineers
will have access to the turbines during flight just as they do in
a surface ship. In the background nestling in a steel cradle, and
surrounded by scaffolding and platforms, is the massive fuselage.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
COPYRIGHT AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4

70 feet high, is being made for Coventry Cathedral by a team
of artists and craftsmen at the Royal College of Arts in
London. Mr Basil Spence, the architect says the designs are
"traditional yet not enormous vitality". The work is being
designed by three artists under the direction of Mr Laurence
Lee, Reader in Stained Glass at the Royal College of Arts.

Photograph shows :- Mr Keith New one of the designers seen
cutting the glass to diagram while Mr L. Lee is seen fitting
the pieces on to the screen.

ESTEN D.H.             1983-5236/73580   21.4.44.
50 M.P.H. ACROBATS THRILL LONDONERS. (Pictures
1000th part of a sec. by ordinary stage lighting).
Ernest Staig and his Flying Australian Air Aces
are at present giving Londoners a thrill with their
novel act at the Circus at the Stoll Theatre.  He
is 27 years old and is assisted by 3 others, Joe
Krzanich, Billy Sawyer and Sid Gimple.  They have
all broken bones of one sort or another in this
50 M.P.H. act. Ernest and his Brother who is a
Flying Officer in the R.A.F. first thought of the
idea in 1933, since when it has, except for a
period when Ernest was in the Army, played all
over Australia and New Zealand.  The Insurance
premium for this act is exceptionally high.
This human roundabout costs over a thousand pounds
and takes 4 hours to erect.  The great problem
at the moment is petrol, and they get an allowance
of 1/2 a pint per day.
OPS.1. Ernest Staig on motor cycle whirls his
companions round at 50 M.P.H. whilst they perform
hair raising acrobatics.

te.text:
BRITAIN is pressing on with plans that will double the
electric power carried to all parts of the country. By a
new method of transmission it should be possible, within a
few years, to meet any demand, and to bring electricity
to every home, farm and factory.
First hint of the new
development appeared in
the first report of the
British Electricity
Authority, which revealed
that experimental work
was in progress to in-
crease the voltages
carried by the transmis-
sion network.
For the past six months
Surrey people have been
puzzled by three gaunt,
bridge-like gantries in a
field near Leatherhead.
Now it can be told that these
gantries are the first signs of
the changing face of Britain—
electric-carrying bridges de-
signed to take the place of the
familiar pylons.
Gas-filled
From these 90 feet high, 120 feet
wide gantries, stationed 400 yards
apart, gas-filled cables will
carry a vastly greater voltage than
the solid cables now slung be-
tween the pylons.
The British grid today cannot
carry more than 132,000 volts.
The new method will make it
possible to transmit 275,000 volts,
more than double the present
supply.
The Surrey experiment has
proved the success of the method.
In the future similar gantries will
cross Britain to form the main
channel of electricity distribution.
First part of the national
scheme will be carried out in the
middle of England.
Work will soon start on a
stretch between West Melton,
[illegible]horne Notts, a
The new pylons for the super-grid system, erected near Leatherhead, Surrey.

GOOD HOUSING DESIGN COMPETITION, 1961 AWARDS
--------------------------------------------

The competition was held by the Ministry of Housing and Local Government
in collaboration with the Royal Institute of British Architects, to promote
the highest standards of design in housing schemes.  Awards were offered
for the best groups of ten or more dwellings built between 31st December 1955
and 31st December 1960.  Either public authorities or private developers
were eligible to compete.
